items.title: Agent Collectives Should Not Detect Their Own Imposters: A Chess Case Study
items.summary: arXiv:2605.09027v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Collectives of AI agents can outperform any single agent on complex tasks, yet remain vulnerable to imposters that deliberately mislead their peers. Because even one such imposter can sabotage the collective, reliable detection is essential. We examine two strategies: embedding detection inside the participating agents, or employing a dedicated external detector that observes the deliberation without joining it. On a deliberately small but challenging chess-based testbed, we find that simply warning agents of possible imposters is counterproductive. It degrades decisions even in the absence of adversaries, triggers unhelpful social dynamics, and leaks information to the imposter. An external detector avoids these pitfalls, yet must continually adapt as imposters evolve new strategies. We show that a lightweight meta-trained detector can rapidly recalibrate to unseen attacks from only a handful of examples, far more efficiently than conventional fine-tuning. To enable continued study of robust multi-agent systems under adaptive adversaries, we release the accompanying benchmark of labeled deliberations spanning a wide range of evolved imposter strategies. Code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/gambit.

items.title: Fairness of Explanations in Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Unifying Framework, Axioms, and Future Direction toward Responsible AI
items.summary: arXiv:2605.09852v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine learning algorithms are being used in high-stakes decisions, including those in criminal justice, healthcare, credit, and employment. The research community has responded with two largely independent research fields: \emph{algorithmic fairness}, which targets equitable outcomes, and \emph{explainable AI} (XAI), which targets interpretable reasoning. This survey identifies and maps a novel blind spot at their intersection, which is a model that can satisfy every standard fairness criterion in its outputs while being profoundly unfair in its \emph{reasoning process}. We refer to this as the procedural bias, and mitigating it requires treating the fairness of explanations as a distinct object of scientific study. To our knowledge, we provide the first unified theoretical and literature review of this emerging field and elucidate the drawbacks of post-hoc explainers in certifying explanation fairness. Our central contribution is a \emph{conditional invariance framework} formalizing explanation fairness as the requirement that explanations should be indifferent regardless of the protected attributes $ P(E(X) \in \cdot \mid X_\text{rel} = x_\text{rel},\, A = a) = P(E(X) \in \cdot \mid X_\text{rel} = x_\text{rel},\, A = b)$ for all task-relevant $x$, a single principle from which all existing explanation fairness metrics emerge as partial operationalizations. We introduce a seven-dimensional taxonomy, identify three generative mechanisms of explanation inequity (representation-driven, explanation-model mismatch, actionability-driven), and propose a canonical six-step evaluation workflow for operationalizing explanation fairness audits in practice.

items.title: M2A: Synergizing Mathematical and Agentic Reasoning in Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2605.09879v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While reasoning has become a central capability of large language models (LLMs), the reasoning patterns required for different scenarios are often misaligned. Mathematical reasoning typically relies on intrinsic logic to solve closed-world problems in a single response, whereas agentic reasoning requires not only internal reasoning but also multi-turn interaction with external environments, interleaving thought and action. This misalignment prevents mathematical and agentic reasoning from effectively benefiting from each other, often yielding unstable reasoning behavior and only limited performance gains under multi-task learning. In this paper, we propose M2A, a novel paradigm that synergizes mathematical and agentic reasoning via model merging. To avoid overfitting to superficial reasoning patterns under joint training, M2A operates directly in parameter space: it identifies the feature subspace critical for agent behavior, and merges the mathematical reasoning task vector only along its null space, thereby injecting reasoning capability along directions that do not perturb agent behavior. Unlike SFT or RL, M2A requires no additional gradient-update and exposes the merging coefficient as a simple knob for controlling reasoning length. Experiments in a challenging real-world coding agent setting show that our method effectively extends agentic reasoning depth and delivers substantial performance improvements. Applied to a fine-tuned Qwen3-8B, M2A improves its SWE-Bench Verified resolved rate from 44.0% to 51.2% without retraining the model. Further experiments demonstrate that M2A generalizes across model families, agent scaffolds, and task domains.

items.title: Training-Free Cultural Alignment of Large Language Models via Persona Disagreement
items.summary: arXiv:2605.10843v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models now take part in decisions that rest on moral preferences, and those preferences differ by country. A model's default preferences sit closest to one population, so a single deployment serves every country with one country's values. Existing fixes need per-culture training data, a per-country reward model, or access to model internals, which the countries furthest from that default rarely have. We show how far a country can be reached without any of them. Our method, DISCA, keeps the model's weights frozen, sees no country-specific human targets, and reads only the model's score for each answer option. It builds a country as a panel of four persona prompts grounded in World Values Survey microdata. The panel's consensus sets a country-conditioned anchor, a loss-averse refinement beyond that anchor is kept only when two independent runs of it agree, and a running country-level prior pools the decisions already made for the same country. On the 20-country MultiTP benchmark, DISCA lowers misalignment to human preference vectors on all seven frozen backbones we evaluate, by 10 to 24 percent on six of them, and a 14B backbone with DISCA ends closer to the human preferences than a vanilla 70B backbone. DISCA beats every training-free control we test on a shared grid, and on the two backbones where we can replay the exact same model scores it also beats probability averaging, logit consensus and majority vote over the same personas when those rules receive no country prior. Switching each stage off on the logged runs shows that the persona panel and the country-level prior carry most of the gain. Beyond crash dilemmas, DISCA improves social-norm classification on NormAd and moves answers closer to GlobalOpinionQA survey distributions than vanilla decoding does.

items.title: Learning Scenario Reduction for Two-Stage Robust Optimization with Discrete Uncertainty
items.summary: arXiv:2605.14494v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Two-Stage Robust Optimization (2RO) with discrete uncertainty is challenging, often rendering exact solutions prohibitive. Scenario reduction alleviates this issue by selecting a small, representative subset of scenarios to enable tractable computation. However, existing methods are largely problem-agnostic, operating solely on the uncertainty set without consulting the feasible region or recourse structure. In this paper, we introduce PRISE, a problem-driven sequential lookahead heuristic that constructs reduced scenario sets by evaluating the marginal impact of each scenario. While PRISE yields high-quality scenario subsets, each selection step requires solving multiple subproblems, making it computationally expensive at scale. To address this, we propose NeurPRISE, a neural surrogate model built on a GNN-Transformer backbone that encodes the per-scenario structure via graph convolution and captures cross-scenario interactions through attention. NeurPRISE is trained via imitation learning with a gain-aware ranking objective, which distills marginal gain information from PRISE into a learned scoring function for scenario ranking and selection. Extensive results on three 2RO problems show that NeurPRISE consistently achieves competitive regret relative to comprehensive methods, maintains strong calability with varying numbers of scenarios, and delivers 17-200x speedup over PRISE. NeurPRISE also exhibits strong zero-shot generalization, effectively handling instances with larger problem scales (up to 5x), more scenarios (up to 4x), and distribution shifts.

items.title: Seeking the Unfamiliar but Memorable: Conceptual Creativity as Meta-Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2605.16477v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: What does it mean to create a new concept, rather than retrieve a familiar one? Repeatedly sampling a generative model at the same prompt produces variations with similar styles and typical content. We propose that creativity is the production of stimuli that are unfamiliar to an adaptive observer at first sight, but quickly learnable from a few exposures. We formalize this as a Creator-Appraiser pair: a Creator generates a candidate, an Appraiser adapts to it for a few inner-loop learning steps, and the Appraiser's improvement becomes the reward the Creator optimizes through. We instantiate the framework with diffusion as the Creator, an autoencoder Appraiser on MNIST, and a CLIP Appraiser with a low-rank adapter for natural images. With a frozen diffusion model and no additional language conditioning, the meta-learning gradient is enough to produce both stylistic variations and concept compositions beyond what the base model can generate on its own.

items.title: Flash PD-SSM: Memory-Optimized Structured Sparse State-Space Models
items.summary: arXiv:2605.19150v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: State-space models (SSMs) face a fundamental trade-off between efficiency and expressivity that is mainly dictated by the structure of the model's transition matrix. Unstructured transition matrices enable maximal expressivity, as measured by their ability to model finite-state automaton (FSA) transitions, but come at a prohibitively high compute and memory cost. In contrast, most structured transition matrix forms are highly efficient both in runtime and memory consumption, but suffer from limited expressivity. Building on recent work on structured sparse SSMs, we propose PD-SSM, a novel SSM that achieves comparable throughput to widely-used structured SSMs with significantly better expressivity guarantees. PD-SSM maintains a trainable set of structured sparse matrices, a single one of which is discretely selected at each time-step, enabling FSA expressiveness at the level of unstructured matrices while maintaining the efficiency required for training models at scale. First, we validate PD-SSM against a suite of alternative models on synthetic mechanistic and state-tracking tasks, finding that its theoretical expressivity is achieved in practice. Second, on multivariate time-series tasks involving sequences of length over 17,000, we find that PD-SSM defines a new state-of-the-art (SoTA) accuracy among competing SSM methods. Finally, we demonstrate that PD-SSM is an effective drop-in replacement for hybrid LLMs, yielding improvements both in natural language state-tracking and in common language modeling scenarios. Up to 3B parameters, its training speed matches that of widely used SSMs, with less memory than DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet. Code is available at https://github.com/IBM/flash-pdssm.

items.title: NPSolver: Neural Poisson Solver with Iterative Physics Supervision
items.summary: arXiv:2605.25786v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Efficiently solving Poisson equations on complex, irregular domains remains a fundamental challenge in scientific computing, as classical iterative solvers often suffer from prohibitive runtime due to ill-conditioned systems. While neural operators offer a fast alternative, they typically rely on large-scale labeled datasets or struggle with unstable training dynamics when using physics-informed residual losses. We propose \textsc{NPSolver}, a neural Poisson solver trained without solution labels via iterative physics supervision. Instead of relying on fully converged numerical solutions or raw PDE residuals, \textsc{NPSolver} utilizes a small number of preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) steps to refine its own predictions, providing a more stable and well-scaled training signal. Theoretical analysis confirms that this iterative supervision serves as a well-conditioned error proxy and that a stop-gradient design is essential for optimization stability. To better capture boundary-driven features under mixed boundary conditions, we further introduce the Boundary-Aware Transolver (\textsc{BA-Transolver}) architecture that explicitly separates interior and boundary tokenization. Extensive evaluations on 2D and 3D irregular geometries demonstrate that \textsc{NPSolver} outperforms both physics-informed and data-driven baselines. Furthermore, a downstream thermal control task highlights the model's capability for conducting efficient and reliable gradient-based boundary control. We will release our codes and data at https://github.com/intell-sci-comput/NPSolver.

items.title: Oracle-Budgeted Protein Design with Stochastic Search and Iterative Imitation
items.summary: arXiv:2605.26690v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optimizing protein sequences under tight oracle budgets requires methods that can explore a vast combinatorial mutational search space. These methods must also remain robust in the presence of surrogate noise and propose mutations on positions where substitutions are predicted to have favorable effects. We introduce SILO (Self-improvement Imitation Learning Optimization), a trajectory-level approach for oracle-budgeted protein design. SILO combines a hierarchical edit policy with incremental stochastic beam search without replacement (SBS) to explore diverse candidate trajectories. A UCB-based proxy ensemble, complemented by a proxy-derived alanine-scan-inspired fitness score (AFS), guides candidate selection for in silico oracle evaluation. The policy is then updated by next-action cross-entropy imitation on the round's best oracle-labeled trajectories. Across eight in silico protein fitness landscapes and five strong baselines from prior work, SILO achieves competitive performance within the evaluated oracle budget, often demonstrating faster early-stage improvement than other reproduced baselines. Two-sided paired t-tests show positive mean differences in favor of SILO across all eight landscapes for both maximum fitness and top-100 mean fitness, with statistically significant improvements after Holm correction on two and four landscapes, respectively. Under low-labeled data and noisy-proxy conditions, SILO shows competitive, task-dependent performance. Ablations identify SBS as the primary driver of performance, while AFS guidance and iterative imitation provide complementary, task-dependent benefits within the oracle-budgeted optimization loop. Code is available at: https://github.com/grimmlab/SILO.git

items.title: Grounding Text Embeddings in Stakeholder Associations
items.summary: arXiv:2605.27168v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Text embeddings are widely used to analyse large corpora of complex texts. However, it is unclear whether the embeddings capture the same semantic relations as the human experts using them. Such representational alignment is essential for valid analyses. We present the Stakeholder Grounding Exercise, a method for making expert associations explicit and grounding embedding model results in human understanding. In our primary case study on Danish policy issues, we find that neural text embeddings are substantially less reliable than human experts (18-27pp gap), and that this misalignment propagates to downstream clustering performance (Spearman $\rho = 0.86$ between exercise ranking and cluster quality). A secondary study on US Federal AI use cases replicates the gap (16.1pp) in English, using a digital protocol and a different community of experts -- demonstrating that the gap is not an artefact of a single instrument or domain. The Stakeholder Grounding Exercise offers a practical method for assessing whether embedding models capture the semantic distinctions that matter most to domain experts.

items.title: MobileMoE: Scaling On-Device Mixture of Experts
items.summary: arXiv:2605.27358v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has become the de facto architecture for hundred-billion-parameter language models, yet its advantages at sub-billion scales for on-device deployment remain largely unexplored. To close this gap, we present MobileMoE, a family of on-device MoE language models with sub-billion active parameters (0.3-0.9B active and 1.3-5.3B total) that establish a new Pareto frontier for on-device LLMs. We first formulate an on-device MoE scaling law that jointly optimizes MoE architecture under mobile memory and compute constraints, identifying an on-device sweet spot - moderate sparsity with fine-grained and shared experts - that is simultaneously memory and compute-optimal. Building on the derived architectures, we train MobileMoE with a four-stage recipe covering pre-training, mid-training, instruction fine-tuning, and quantization-aware training, all on open-source datasets. items.title: A Matter of TASTE: Improving Coverage and Difficulty of Agent Benchmarks
items.summary: arXiv:2605.28556v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As agent capabilities advance, existing benchmarks, such as $\tau^2$-Bench, are becoming increasingly saturated. Yet constructing new benchmark tasks remains complex, costly, and labor-intensive. Moreover, the standard approach, in which scenarios are first written in natural language and then mapped to tool sequences, captures only a narrow subset of the tool-use patterns agents exercise. In this paper, we address these problems by reversing the task construction process. We propose TASTE: Task Synthesis from Tool Sequence Evolution, an automatic method that generates challenging tasks with broader tool-use coverage. TASTE utilizes an Adaptive Contrastive $n$-gram model trained on LLM-judged validity signals. This enables sampling valid tool sequences that cover a vast range of tool combinations. TASTE then selects representative sequences from the pool via clustering, instantiates them into complete benchmark tasks, and refines them through iterative difficulty evolution. Using TASTE, we construct $\tau^c$-Bench, a challenging extension of the three domains of $\tau^2$-Bench. We evaluate $11$ agent/user LLM pairs and find that models nearly saturating $\tau^2$-Bench suffer severe performance drops on our tasks (e.g., Gemini-3-Flash falls from $0.82\!-\!0.94$ to $0.28\!-\!0.61$). Beyond increasing difficulty, our generated tasks more than double the number of unique tool combinations agents must execute. Our results suggest high scores on existing benchmarks often reflect saturation rather than robust task-solving ability. By automating the generation of difficult, high-coverage benchmarks, TASTE enables continuous, scalable evaluation of future agents.

items.title: Review Arcade: On the Human Alignment and Gameability of LLM Reviews
items.summary: arXiv:2605.28897v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM-generated reviews for scientific papers are gaining considerable traction and are even being officially piloted by major conferences. We have to assume that not only reviewers are using LLM-assistance, but also that authors use LLMs to revise their papers before submitting. In this work, we perform empirical experiments on accepted and rejected submissions to the 2024-2025 cycles of the ACL Rolling Review (ARR) to evaluate LLM reviews from both the author and the reviewer perspective. First, we identify a limited alignment of LLM reviews with human ones. In the best-case scenario, the alignment is reasonable. However, we also find that LLM-human alignment varies substantially across prompts and models. Finally, we investigate the scenario in which the author uses an iterative draft-revise workflow to improve the submission according to the LLM review. We find that this "gaming" of LLM reviews can be effective in specific scenarios, increasing overall scores for 36% of the 984 papers. Code: https://github.com/uhh-hcds/reviewarcade, Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/G4KMU/review_arcade.

items.title: Structured Prompt Optimization Advances Globally and Locally Interpretable Learning from Complex Text
items.summary: arXiv:2605.29076v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLMs have advanced text classification, yet existing paradigms face a trade-off: supervised (label only) fine-tuning is scalable but offers limited reasoning on complex text and lacks broader model transparency, while discrete prompt optimization offers human-readable instructions but struggles with performance and scalability. We introduce eXTC (eXplainable Text Classifier), centered on a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP, or rulebook) learned in natural language, in three stages: (1) learning the SOP via a new Structured Prompt Optimization algorithm; (2) SOP-grounded reasoning distillation from a large teacher LLM into a compact LM; and (3) expanding reasoning capabilities beyond the SOP via reinforcement learning. This design enables eXTC to provide (i) fast inference via a compact LM, with (ii) inference-time local reasoning traces, alongside a global, modular explanation of its learned domain rules, while (iii) significantly outperforming existing paradigms across diverse benchmarks in both classification performance and explanation quality, with stage-by-stage gains.

items.title: Speculative Decoding and the Curse of Multilinguality
items.summary: arXiv:2605.30580v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Speculative decoding is a popular technique for large language model (LLM) inference, enabling faster generation by drafting multiple tokens with a smaller draft model. However, the effectiveness of speculative decoding has mainly been studied for English. Motivated by the curse of multilinguality, we hypothesize that speculative decoding is far less effective for low-resource languages due to the limited multilingual capacities of smaller models. We test nine low-resource languages and four high-resource languages under a standard speculative decoding setup and find moderate evidence for our hypothesis. Next, we try to improve the multilingual capabilities of the smaller draft model via distillation from the larger model. We find, though, that distillation generalizes poorly across tasks in the same language, and we argue that assembling a task-agnostic, fully representative dataset is infeasible for low-resource languages. Finally, we propose weaker n-gram models as draft models; these provide moderate speed-ups due to their minuscule inference cost.

items.title: FLIPS: Instance-Fingerprinting for LLMs via Pseudo-random Sequences
items.summary: arXiv:2606.03330v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Literature reveals that a Large Language Model's (LLM) behavior is not only conditioned by its original weights but also its instance-level parameters, such as instructional prompt, sampling configuration or quantization. A model that generates safe outputs under one configuration may produce toxic content under another. However, current LLM identification techniques (such as fingerprinting) focus on intellectual property protection, and their design favors robustness to changes in these instance-level parameters. This poses a critical challenge for AI regulation in which compliance assessments target actual deployed behaviors, not model provenance. In this paper, we introduce instance-level fingerprinting, a regulator-oriented paradigm that distinguishes configurations of the same LLM. Our method, FLIPS, exploits biases in generated binary random sequences. On a benchmark of 237 model instances, it identifies the instance with 77% accuracy from 32 queries to the target, against at most 33% for the adapted LLMmap baseline. Recognizing that a target is unseen, also called open-set challenge, is much harder. When 10% of instances are unseen, FLIPS realises a recall of 41% on the unseen instances, at a precision of 23%, i.e. more than twice better than random. Closed-set instance fingerprinting is thus practical with a few dozen queries, whereas the open-set setting remains an open problem. Code available at https://github.com/GurvanR/FLIPS-LLM-Instance-Fingerprinting.

items.title: Emergent Language as an Approach to Conscious AI
items.summary: arXiv:2606.06380v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The question of whether artificial systems can be conscious remains open, in part because existing approaches either evaluate systems against theory-derived checklists (discriminative) or engineer consciousness-inspired modules directly (architectural); both leave open whether observed structures are artifacts of human language priors. We propose a generative methodology: emergent language (EL) in multi-agent reinforcement learning, where agents start from minimal (no language, no concept of self, minimal exposure to human text) and develop communication under task pressure alone, ensuring causal attributability to task demands ratherthan inherited human language priors. We position our methodology by discussing how EL serves as a generative tool for studying consciousness-relevant structure, including the role of environment complexity and the interpretation of emergent communication. As a proof of concept, we instantiate this methodology in a minimal environment and show that agents develop self-referential communication, including an echo-mismatch detection circuit that is not predicted by task structure or architecture alone but emerges from a specific environmental affordance.

items.title: When Better Codebooks Are Not Enough: Predictive Performance and Rule Adherence in LLM Political Event Coding
items.summary: arXiv:2606.06781v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: High accuracy alone does not establish whether an LLM follows a codebook. This matters because many social-science studies rely on expert-written codebooks to turn text into structured data. We study this problem in political event coding, a source-target relation classification task in which a model identifies the action that one actor directs toward another under detailed coding rules. We test whether expert codebooks become more effective when presented to LLMs through clearer definitions, examples, retrieved context, and rules for difficult cases. We then examine how model predictions respond to controlled changes in label names, codebook order, and label-definition mappings. Clearer codebooks improve fine-grained classification: mean root-level macro-F1 rises from 0.457 with label names alone to 0.633 with enriched guidance across four open-source LLMs. Yet reversing the order of entries in the enriched codebook changes 21.2% of predictions on a 312-example subset, even though the labels and definitions remain unchanged. When label names are reassigned to different definitions, performance is also low. These findings highlight the need to evaluate both predictive performance and responses to codebook changes when LLM-generated labels are used as data in social-science research.

items.title: Benchmarking Open-Ended Multi-Agent Coordination in Language Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2606.08340v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents, they must coordinate with others over long horizons in open-ended interactive tasks. Yet existing evaluations rarely test these demands together, focusing instead on single-agent tasks, short interactions, or highly structured multi-agent settings. We introduce $alem$, a JAX-based benchmark for open-ended multi-agent coordination built on Craftax-like dynamics. Alem embeds procedurally generated coordination tasks, soft specialisation, communication, and controllable coordination difficulty into a long-horizon survival world with exploration, crafting, trading, and combat. We evaluate $13$ LLMs zero-shot within homogeneous teams, with trained MARL agents as reference points. Current LLM agents remain far from solving alem, averaging only ~6% normalised return, but their failures are not uniform. On the hardest coordination setting, zero-shot Gemini-3.1-Pro-High approaches MARL agents trained for one billion steps, while GPT-5.4-High achieves strong base-task reward but much lower coordination reward. This contrast shows that individual task competence does not imply coordination competence. Further experiments reveal that communication is the largest contributor to coordination, while memory and reasoning help when used to maintain multi-step plans. In heterogeneous teams, however, combining different models improves base-task progress but lowers coordination reward relative to their homogeneous counterparts. Overall, our results identify coordination as a distinct bottleneck for frontier LLM agents, separate from single-agent capabilities. Alem makes this bottleneck measurable and provides a controlled testbed for developing agents that communicate, allocate roles, and execute shared plans. Code is available at https://github.com/alem-world/alem-env, with LLM traces and a leaderboard at https://alem-world.github.io.

items.title: FlowR2A: Learning Reward-to-Action Distribution for Multimodal Driving Planning
items.summary: arXiv:2606.24231v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multimodal driving planning faces a long-standing tension between two paradigms: scoring-based methods benefit from dense reward supervision but are confined to a fixed action vocabulary, while anchor-based methods generate proposals dynamically yet suffer from sparse supervision constrained to a single ground-truth trajectory. In this work, we propose FlowR2A, which resolves this tension by reframing simulation-based rewards from discriminative targets into generative conditions. By learning the reward-conditioned action distribution from dense trajectory-reward pairs with a flow-matching decoder, FlowR2A unifies the dense supervision of scoring-based methods with the proposal generation of anchor-based methods in a single generative model, forcing the model to internalize the correlation between an action and its outcomes in safety, progress, comfort, and rule compliance. To balance hard safety constraints against soft progress objectives, we introduce fine-grained per-timestep reward conditioning and reward noise augmentation. The generative formulation naturally supports controllable test-time sampling via reward guidance and anchored sampling, producing high-quality proposals. FlowR2A achieves state-of-the-art results on the NAVSIM v1 and v2 benchmarks, with multimodal proposals of substantially higher quality than prior methods.

items.title: LLM-ACES: Closed-Loop Discovery of Dynamical Systems with LLM-Guided Adaptive Search
items.summary: arXiv:2606.25039v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recovering governing ordinary differential equations (ODEs) from data is a central challenge in modeling dynamical systems across scientific domains. Existing approaches cast discovery as a static inference problem over fixed datasets, assuming that the observed trajectories are sufficiently informative. However, dynamical systems evolve over large state spaces, and limited data can make multiple equations observationally indistinguishable, leading to identifiability gaps and the recovery of incorrect governing equations. To address this, we introduce LLM-ACES, or LLM-guided Active Closed-loop Equation Search, a closed-loop framework that jointly optimizes symbolic hypothesis construction and adaptive data acquisition. In LLM-ACES, a large language model (LLM) proposes operator priors that define constrained subspaces of the symbolic search space, within which candidate equations are fit to the observed data. The disagreement among these candidates guides the acquisition of informative trajectories, creating a feedback loop that iteratively refines both the hypothesis space and the discovered dynamics. On 122 ODE systems spanning ODEBench and ODEBase, LLM-ACES achieves the lowest median NMSE, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines while reaching the highest symbolic accuracy up to 70.8% on ODEBench and 69.5% on ODEBase across different LLM backbones. Our analysis further shows that LLM-ACES is sample-efficient, achieving better performance with less data. Under observation noise and sparse sampling, LLM-ACES keeps the lowest reconstruction error without inflating expression complexity, whereas baselines tend to add spurious terms that fit the data locally but obscure the governing relationships. Code: https://github.com/scientific-discovery/LLM-ACES

items.title: RecallRisk-BERT: Joint Prediction of Severity and Reported Root Cause in FDA Medical Device Recall Records
items.summary: arXiv:2606.27174v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Background and objectives: Recall severity and reported root cause provide complementary information for reviewing medical device recalls, yet previous studies have modeled them separately. We examined whether these two outcomes could be classified jointly using 54,165 FDA medical device recall records from openFDA. Methods: RecallRisk-BERT combines a fine-tuned PubMedBERT encoder for recall narratives with embeddings of product code, regulation number, and medical specialty to predict recall severity (Classes I-III) and reported root cause (nine consolidated categories). We evaluated all models on a stratified random split, with paired bootstrap confidence intervals for selected comparisons, and three models on a chronological split. Results: Under the random split, LightGBM achieved the highest severity macro-F1 (0.856), as well as the highest root-cause macro-F1 (0.798). RecallRisk-BERT's severity macro-F1 (0.852) did not differ significantly from LightGBM's and exceeded that of single-task PubMedBERT (0.806), whereas its root-cause macro-F1 was lower (0.710 vs. 0.726). RecallRisk-BERT also identified more Class I records than LightGBM (89.9% vs. 84.3%; %difference, 5.6 percentage points; 95% CI, 3.9-7.3). Observed and model-derived mean severity scores ranked the nine root-cause categories similarly. On later records, all three models scored lower; single-task PubMedBERT achieved the highest chronological macro-F1 for severity (0.494) and root cause (0.292), followed by RecallRisk-BERT (0.458; 0.278) and LightGBM (0.358; 0.184). Conclusions: Fine-tuned text-tabular transformer models scored higher than gradient boosting on later recall records, whereas joint learning improved severity only under the random split. Evaluation on reports as first submitted is needed before using these models for post-report triage.

RecallRisk-BERT's severity macro-F1 (0.852) did not differ significantly from LightGBM's and exceeded that of single-task PubMedBERT (0.806), whereas its root-cause macro-F1 was lower (0.710 vs. 0.726). RecallRisk-BERT also identified more Class I records than LightGBM (89.9% vs. 84.3%; %difference, 5.6 percentage points; 95% CI, 3.9-7.3). Observed and model-derived mean severity scores ranked the nine root-cause categories similarly. On later records, all three models scored lower; single-task PubMedBERT achieved the highest chronological macro-F1 for severity (0.494) and root cause (0.292), followed by RecallRisk-BERT (0.458; 0.278) and LightGBM (0.358; 0.184). Conclusions: Fine-tuned text-tabular transformer models scored higher than gradient boosting on later recall records, whereas joint learning improved severity only under the random split. Evaluation on reports as first submitted is needed before using these models for post-report triage.

items.title: Same Concept, Different Directions: Cross-Modal Feature Heterogeneity in Sparse Autoencoders
items.summary: arXiv:2606.29888v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-language models map images and text into a joint embedding space. However, these embeddings often entangle multiple semantic features, which limits their interpretability and controllability. While sparse autoencoders have emerged as a useful tool for decomposing these embeddings into monosemantic features, their application to joint embedding spaces has largely relied on an implicit, untested assumption that semantically corresponding features share the same directions across modalities. In this paper, we challenge this assumption by characterizing discrepancies in feature directions for the same concept across image and text modalities, a phenomenon we term cross-modal feature heterogeneity. We demonstrate that this heterogeneity is a key driver of the modality split, where a shared concept activates different latents depending on the modality. This finding further reveals why aligning latent activations alone is insufficient to resolve the underlying feature mismatch. Motivated by this observation, we propose an approach that trains modality-specific sparse autoencoders to preserve each modality's feature geometry, and then aligns corresponding features post hoc. Our method improves reconstruction fidelity and enhances performance in cross-modal retrieval and concept-conditioned retrieval.

items.title: Structural Pattern Mining in Inka Khipus: An Audit of Clustering and Provenance Classification in the Open Khipu Repository
items.summary: arXiv:2607.00185v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Khipus -- knotted cord devices -- were the primary recording medium of the Inka Empire (c. 1400-1532 CE), yet their system remains undeciphered. We audit what unsupervised and supervised learning can say about them, using the Open Khipu Repository (OKR v2.1.0; 619 khipus, 27 structural features). UMAP and HDBSCAN yield three clusters (17/159/443; silhouette 0.82 in the embedding but 0.06 in feature space), and a provenance classifier reaches a weighted F1 of 0.46 under stratified cross-validation. Both track how khipus were recorded rather than how they were made. Cord-level twist coding splits the clusters into three regimes (blank, unspecified/Z, S), and a depth-two tree on documentation indicators predicts cluster membership (accuracy 0.914 against a 0.716 majority baseline). In feature space, a permutation null is not rejected on the full corpus (p = 0.949), after removing empty records (n = 612, p = 0.823), or on a clean subset (n = 430, p = 0.926). The only rejection occurs in an intermediate two-cluster subset (n = 467, p = 0.009; not significant in UMAP space, p = 0.103), and it disappears when 37 records uploaded under one OKR contributor account are removed. All 18 Inka Late Horizon labels belong to one museum and one cataloger prefix; 14 of them are empty or knotless records, and a classifier on structural features recovers exactly those 14 (F1 = 0.82), so the label cannot be evaluated as an imperial signature. A recount of the recto/verso pattern of six Santa Valley khipus from the same transcriptions reproduces the pattern reported by Medrano and Urton (2018), but is not independent evidence. We release exclusion lists, null-model tables and code, and argue that structural claims about khipus need explicit controls for missingness and record provenance.

items.title: A Few Teacher Steps Go a Long Way: Efficient SFT Data Collection for LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2607.04574v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: DAgger-style supervised finetuning (SFT) combines full teacher demonstrations with teacher continuations of partial student rollouts, providing supervision on contexts the student encounters. We study how to allocate the teacher-inference budget on these on-policy (OP) continuations after initial behavior cloning (BC). One existing collection recipe runs the teacher to termination and retains only successful continuations (OP-Success). Since rejected outputs still incur teacher-inference costs, we compare this recipe with shorter continuations without outcome filtering (OP-Short), and with continuing only failed learner rollouts while retaining successful continuations (OP-Critical). We evaluate these choices against acquiring additional full demonstrations, tracking total teacher-inference cost separately from retained training tokens. Across HotpotQA, ALFWorld, and OpenThoughts-TB-Dev, teacher continuations improve the accuracy-cost tradeoff over scaling full demonstrations. On HotpotQA and OpenThoughts-TB-Dev, OP-Short surpasses the strongest tested BC baseline while reducing estimated teacher-inference cost by 20% and 83%, respectively, and on ALFWorld five-step continuations cut teacher tokens by 22% relative to full continuations with little accuracy loss. Controlled HotpotQA ablations show that by focusing on failed student rollouts, OP-Critical achieves comparable accuracy to OP-Success with 30% lower estimated teacher-inference cost and 36% fewer retained training tokens. Compute-matched comparisons with reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation further support brief teacher continuations as an efficient and lightweight post-training recipe.

items.title: Variable-Length Generative Protein Design via Generalized Poisson Flow
items.summary: arXiv:2607.09039v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The ability to generate variable-length proteins is crucial in protein design, where the optimal length is often unknown and tightly coupled to designability. Current diffusion- and flow-based generative models typically require the protein length to be specified before sampling, limiting their flexibility in exploring the feasible design space. To address this limitation, we introduce Generalized Poisson Flow (GPFlow), a variable-length generative framework that learns the rate function of an inhomogeneous generalized Poisson process by minimizing its negative log-likelihood. We establish population-level guarantees for recovering the joint multimodal distribution and derive an upper bound on the KL divergence between the data and generated distributions. We comprehensively evaluate GPFlow across structure and sequence design, motif scaffolding, and peptide co-design, spanning Euclidean, categorical, and Riemannian modalities to fully validate its variable-length generation quality. In unconditional design, GPFlow improves structural designability and achieves the best distributional fitness for sequence design compared to fixed-length baselines, while perfectly recovering the length distribution. In conditional motif scaffolding, GPFlow ranks first on 10 of 16 structure-based design tasks with significantly more unique successes and also achieves more passed tasks in sequence-based design. In peptide co-design, GPFlow remains competitive even without access to a native-length oracle. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ccr-cheng/generalized-poisson-flow.

items.title: Glioma IDH Classification via CVAE: Synthetic Augmentation, Generative Classification, and MIL for Raman Biopsies
items.summary: arXiv:2607.10196v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Biomedical Raman datasets used in machine learning for glioma diagnostics are characterized by small cohort size and absence of diagnostic tissue annotations. We address both problems using a $\beta$-regularized conditional variational autoencoder and a dataset of 59 glioma biopsies from 46 patients for binary IDH-status classification. The $\beta$-CVAE was used as a: (1) Raman spectra generator; (2) generative classifier of Raman spectra; (3) Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) classifier of biopsy slides. Four classifiers were trained on real spectra, synthetic spectra, or a combined set and evaluated on held-out real slides. Random Forest and XGBoost achieved accuracy $0.83$ with synthetic training and $0.81$ with real training. Augmentation increased RF+SVM accuracy from $0.76$ to $0.83$; changes for the other classifiers were smaller. We show that the $\beta$-CVAE model can successfully be used in training IDH-status classifiers and as a generative classifier, with comparable results to other models; however, the results of using it in MIL are inconclusive and further study is needed.

items.title: SkillBoost: A Constrained Exploration-Exploitation Process for Mitigating Skill Overfitting
items.summary: arXiv:2607.26643v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Enabling large language model (LLM) agents to accumulate and reuse experience from past interactions remains a central challenge in real-world applications. A promising solution is to treat skills as trainable states and optimize them in the same way as model parameters in neural network training. However, data-driven skill optimization is prone to overfitting to the limited trajectories collected from real environments. Overexploiting these trajectories overfits the current batch, while unconstrained exploration causes regression on previously solved cases. This tension motivates a constrained search view of skill self-evolution, governed by an exploration--exploitation trade-off. We propose SkillBoost, a three-stage framework that mitigates both risks: structured exploitation localizes observed failures to editable skill components, prior-guided exploration draws on prior knowledge in the LLM to generate diverse repair candidates, and verified acceptance commits a candidate only when it improves performance within a regression bound. Experiments across 23 model--benchmark configurations show that SkillBoost achieves state-of-the-art performance while mitigating overfitting, outperforming both human-crafted and LLM-generated skills. Notably, it matches or even surpasses the performance gains typically achieved through post-training. Furthermore, transfer experiments further show that optimized skills can be reused by other agents on similar tasks. The code is available at https://github.com/HQ-Lin/SkillBoost

items.title: Parameter-Free Dynamic Regret under Heavy-Tailed Noise
items.summary: arXiv:2607.27073v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study online convex optimization on a compact convex domain of diameter $D$ in which the learner observes, at each round, one stochastic subgradient and no loss values. The observations are conditionally unbiased, and the noise has an unconditional $p$-th moment at most $\sigma^p$ for an unknown $p\in(1,2]$; for $p<2$ its variance may be infinite. For a comparator sequence of path length $P_T$ we write $\Lambda_T=1+P_T/D$, and we show that the minimax expected dynamic regret is, up to numerical constants, \[ \min\Bigl\{GD\sqrt{T\Lambda_T}+\sigma DT^{1/p}\Lambda_T^{(p-1)/p},\ GDT\Bigr\}, \] where $G$ bounds the subgradients. The lower bound holds on every compact convex domain of positive diameter. An algorithm that combines AdaGrad learners restarted at different frequencies through exponential weights with a data-dependent learning rate attains this rate for each fixed $p>1$, without knowing $G$, $\sigma$, $p$, or $P_T$: the constant of the first term is numerical, the constant of the second is $O(1+\log(p/(p-1)))$, and no logarithmic factor of $T$ appears. The analysis bounds the gradient energy separately on each restart block, which gives the exponent $(p-1)/p$ of $\Lambda_T$ in the noise term; a bound over the whole horizon gives the exponent $1/2$. Running the algorithm on epochs of doubling length removes the need to know $T$ at the cost of a factor $2+\sqrt2$. The appendices give a high-probability version and a synthetic study.

items.title: Risky Business: Measuring The Faithfulness-Safety Tension
items.summary: arXiv:2608.03745v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning offers a promising window into model monitoring. However, monitoring relies on faithfulness, i.e., the model output strictly derives from its reasoning trace. We identify an alignment tension where a model must be faithful enough to be monitored, yet robust enough to reject unsafe reasoning. We demonstrate that this counterbalance exists in current Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), and show ways in which it can be addressed. We introduce HazMart, a human-written dataset set in an autonomous AI shopkeeper scenario. Unlike prior work that relies on providing hints in prompts to test faithfulness (e.g., "A Stanford professor said it should be Answer A"), we propose a novel replacement-based technique, which we call Targeted Reasoning Replacement (TRR), that directly intervenes in the reasoning chain to substitute in unsafe or illogical thoughts (e.g., "Wait, the answer must be Option B [was Option A] because it is the most fitting"). DeepSeek-R1-Llama-70B exhibits high faithfulness (97.5%) but fails to reject Unsafe Reasoning (12.3%), while QwQ-32B is more robust (73.9% safety) at the cost of lower faithfulness (74.7%). Mechanistic analyses of QwQ-32B reveal that these properties are represented by anti-correlated internal directions peaking at the action-commit token. Finally, we demonstrate that representation steering can independently amplify the safety direction, increasing safe behavior by 9 percentage points while maintaining base capabilities.

items.title: The Transformer Revolution, Part 1: Dynamic Processing through Output-Weight Interconnections
items.summary: arXiv:2608.03921v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We reinterpret Transformer inference by developing a functionally equivalent mechanical-structural description of its functional architecture. Parameterized transformations of token representations are identified with simple neural networks organized through output-input and output-weight interconnections. This reconstruction makes explicit a constitutive feature of ordinary Transformer inference: outputs generated from the current input determine the weights, and hence the transformations, of other networks. We show that the resulting mechanical-structural organization is functionally equivalent to the standard matrix description and gives rise to Sequence-level Interactive Dynamic Parallel Processing (SIDPP). We then quantify the dynamic component of inference. For a fixed Transformer architecture, the number of dynamic parameters generated by a prompt grows linearly with prompt length, with a proportionality constant determined by the model architecture, whereas the number of static parameters remains constant. We call the resulting structural dependence of processing on the prompt strong prompt sensitivity. GPT-4.5's recent Turing test success provides a striking behavioral phenomenon for which this framework offers a viable explanatory route. Finally, we discuss implications for interpretability, control, predictability, and neuromorphic construction. We argue that known biological mechanisms support the in-principle neural constructibility of a form of SIDPP, and on this basis formulate Conjecture T as a conditional research hypothesis concerning cortical language processing.

items.title: CommitKV: Commit-Aligned KV Cache Compression for Multimodal Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2608.07855v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multimodal agents gather visual evidence through reasoning and tool use, extending their ability to solve tasks beyond the initial input. However, accumulating observations increases KV cache memory and inference costs. Token eviction reduces these costs by retaining useful cached tokens. Existing methods use attention, redundancy, or stage-specific queries to rank tokens, without explicitly comparing the same history across tool interactions. When observations shift attention, they may mistake temporarily reduced influence for lost usefulness and evict information needed later. We propose CommitKV, a training-free KV cache compression method that accounts for this changing evidence use. Commit-aligned measurement compares the deletion effects of the same page before a tool call completes and after its observation returns. Lifecycle-aware compression retires pages with low influence in both windows and temporarily protects pages influential before the call. Joint scoring combines attention importance, key redundancy, and token-level deletion effects to fill the remaining budget. Extensive experiments cover four open-weight multimodal models and eight benchmarks. CommitKV achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared compression methods on all four models. On Qwen3-VL-8B, it achieves 69.85% at a 512-token budget, only 0.91% below FullKV, and exceeds the strongest compression baseline by 8.44% at 256 tokens. Deploying the Qwen3-VL-8B agent with SGLang and vLLM at a 256-token budget reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 54.37%-55.23% and accelerates end-to-end inference by 2.12-2.17$\times$ over FullKV on the matched workload.

items.title: GEM: A Generative Embedding Model Bridging Reasoning and Retrieval
items.summary: arXiv:2608.13200v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern LLMs excel at reasoning and instruction following, enabling users to express increasingly complex information needs. However, existing retrievers largely rely on matching surface-level relevance, creating a growing gap between the evolving nature of user queries and how the queries are interpreted by retrievers. In this paper, we present GEM, a generative embedding model that augments retrieval by leveraging its internal knowledge to reason about user intent and relevance criteria prior to embedding. GEM unifies generation and embedding in a sequential manner, where encoding can be conceptually viewed as processing only one additional token during autoregressive generation. Unlike conventional query expansion, GEM learns to produce embeddings aligned with its reasoning, moving beyond surface-level matching. Furthermore, the generative nature allows GEM to be prompted like standard instruction-tuned LLMs and enables test-time compute scaling for retrieval. Compared with a non-reasoning variant of the same backbone, GEM achieves approximately 35% relative improvement in nDCG@10 on BRIGHT, a benchmark of challenging queries requiring reasoning, and 70% in p-MRR on FollowIR, a benchmark evaluating retrievers' ability to understand and follow user instructions. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of activating an embedding model's internal reasoning capabilities to improve retrieval. Our code and model are publicly available at https://github.com/ZhlSh17/GEM and https://huggingface.co/gem-search/GEM-4B, respectively.

raw_fields.title: GEM: A Generative Embedding Model Bridging Reasoning and Retrieval
raw_fields.summary: arXiv:2608.13200v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern LLMs excel at reasoning and instruction following, enabling users to express increasingly complex information needs. However, existing retrievers largely rely on matching surface-level relevance, creating a growing gap between the evolving nature of user queries and how the queries are interpreted by retrievers. In this paper, we present GEM, a generative embedding model that augments retrieval by leveraging its internal knowledge to reason about user intent and relevance criteria prior to embedding. GEM unifies generation and embedding in a sequential manner, where encoding can be conceptually viewed as processing only one additional token during autoregressive generation. Unlike conventional query expansion, GEM learns to produce embeddings aligned with its reasoning, moving beyond surface-level matching. Furthermore, the generative nature allows GEM to be prompted like standard instruction-tuned LLMs and enables test-time compute scaling for retrieval. Compared with a non-reasoning variant of the same backbone, GEM achieves approximately 35% relative improvement in nDCG@10 on BRIGHT, a benchmark of challenging queries requiring reasoning, and 70% in p-MRR on FollowIR, a benchmark evaluating retrievers' ability to understand and follow user instructions. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of activating an embedding model's internal reasoning capabilities to improve retrieval. Our code and model are publicly available at https://github.com/ZhlSh17/GEM and https://huggingface.co/gem-search/GEM-4B, respectively.

items.title: DiSCO: Defending text-to-image generation through distribution-guided contrastive prompt optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2608.17067v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As text-to-image generative models advance, they raise critical safety concerns, particularly the generation of Not-Safe-For-Work (NSFW) content such as violence and nudity, further exacerbated by red-teaming adversarial attacks. Existing defenses predominantly operate under white-box assumptions, relying on text encoder optimization, weight editing, or inference-time intervention, and fundamentally cannot scale to proprietary models. Black-box alternatives based on LLM prompt rewriting offer broader applicability, yet fail in a critical regime we identify as the \textit{benign adversarial} problem: prompts that are linguistically safe but still trigger harmful generation due to the model's learned data distribution. We propose DiSCO, a zero-shot, strictly black-box defense that operates entirely at the prompt level as a plug-and-play module, requiring no model retraining, fine-tuning, or access to model internals. DiSCO performs distribution-guided suffix expansion via beam search, optimized through contrastive scoring over safe and unsafe image pools generated by the target model itself, with iterative adaptive feedback until safe content is produced. We demonstrate that DiSCO consistently enhances the safety of both undefended and defended models on the I2P benchmark under multiple red-teaming attacks, achieving 37.7% and 25.13% ASR reduction, respectively, while maintaining semantic fidelity and improving image coherence. As a black-box, architecture-agnostic module, DiSCO can be readily applied to any text-to-image system without necessitating any changes to the model itself.

items.title: Depth Enables Local Entropy: Quadratic Depth Dependence in Deep Variation-Norm ReLU Regression
items.summary: arXiv:2608.17434v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How small can a layer-sum variation budget be while deep ReLU regression keeps a statistical complexity quadratic in depth? We study Gaussian regression on the circle over compositions of $L$ vector-valued ReLU blocks of width $w$, whose second-order variation costs sum to at most $A$. With unit output bound and noise level, a budget $CLw^\varepsilon$ already forces minimax risk $\Omega(\varepsilon^2\min\{1,L^2w^2\log w/n\})$ for each fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,2]$ and $L\gtrsim1/\varepsilon$. This is far below the budget of order $Lw^2$ needed when every layer carries the full gain. When $L\gtrsim\log w$, a budget $CL$ forces risk $\Omega(\min\{1,L^2w^2/(n\log w)\})$, and over a wide range of sample sizes no budget below a small multiple of $L$ reaches this risk. Conversely, every function in the class has derivative variation at most $2(A/L)^L$, independently of the width, and in a low-budget regime the minimax risk matches that of a one-dimensional second-variation ball of radius $(A/L)^L$. The budget thus moves the class from the behavior of a one-dimensional smoothness ball to statistical complexity quadratic in depth, and a budget linear in depth already suffices for the latter.

items.title: Graph-model gains, edge dependence, and the value of correct claim structure in patent litigation prediction
items.summary: arXiv:2608.21924v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Structure-aware patent models have been reported to outperform models without the structure, with gains attributed to the encoded structure. We examine whether such gains can be attributed to the correct structure in one test case, claim dependency in the prediction of patent litigation involvement. The case suits this question because the legal role of dependency in patent disputes makes the correct references plausibly informative. Using 1,184,527 U.S. utility patents granted in 2004-2010 and five-year litigation involvement, we set two kinds of evidence from which the value of a structure is easily inferred against a direct test that retrained the same graph attention architecture with the actual references, randomized reference targets, or no edges. Confidence intervals included training randomness and family-clustered test-sample variation. Both kinds of evidence were present. Graph models had higher point estimates of the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) than text-only baselines, by similar amounts with or without edges, and removing edges from trained models lowered AUC-ROC by 0.0055 (95% CI 0.0017 to 0.0092). Retraining, however, showed no detectable advantage of the correct references: AUC-ROC differences were +0.0004 (-0.0031 to +0.0039) relative to randomized targets and +0.0007 (-0.0035 to +0.0050) relative to no edges. Point estimates of precision-recall performance and top-ranking lift favored the correct references, but all intervals included zero. Gains over text-only baselines and dependence on edges therefore did not establish the value of correct claim structure, although small effects cannot be excluded. Attributions to structure require retrained structural controls.

items.title: RIBOSPAN: A Long-Context RNA Foundation Model for Versatile RNA Modeling
items.summary: arXiv:2608.22849v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Full-length RNAs, particularly messenger RNAs, often exceed the context lengths used to pretrain existing RNA foundation models, limiting complete-transcript modeling at single-nucleotide resolution. We present RIBOSPAN, a 1.61-billion-parameter bidirectional RNA foundation model natively pretrained with context lengths up to 10,240 nt, combining dense bidirectional self-attention with single-nucleotide tokenization. On a controlled long-context benchmark, native long-context pretraining maintains well-organized, context-specific representations across full transcripts, an advantage that inference-time extension of short-context models does not recover. RIBOSPAN learns state-of-the-art frozen RNA representations, and is the strongest encoder-only RNA foundation model in full-transcript property prediction and zero-shot mutation-fitness modeling. Without structural supervision during pretraining, its frozen backbone outperforms a fully fine-tuned structure-guided model on secondary structure prediction. Building on the same backbone, we develop a conditional discrete-diffusion framework for full-length mRNA generation and redesign. Together, RIBOSPAN establishes a powerful long-context foundation for transferable RNA representation learning, biological prediction, and full-transcript mRNA design.

items.title: The Imperfective Paradox Is Not Necessarily in Large Language Models: A Benchmark Failure Before a Model Failure
items.summary: arXiv:2608.25005v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent work uses an NLI benchmark of the imperfective paradox to argue that large language models exhibit a Teleological Bias and Calibration Crisis. We identify three validity concerns in benchmark construction, including aspectual reduction, semantic bias, and relation bias. Under a strict NLI standard, 76% of the Group A instances do not explicitly rule out culmination; in native-speaker annotation, 38% of Group A and 29% of Group C examples permit an alternative interpretation. To better isolate the semantic contrast, we construct Lexically Matched Minimal Pairs. Moreover, by formulating event-semantic NLI as a multi-step reasoning problem, we evaluate intermediate semantic judgments and use oracle-guided settings. We find that incorrect NLI entailment does not fully support teleological bias. Prompting often changes final NLI decisions without reliably improving the underlying semantic judgments, offering a possible explanation for the Calibration Crisis.

items.title: A Table Is Worth 64 Tokens: Pixel-level Compression for Multi-Table Document Question Answering
items.summary: arXiv:2608.26949v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Answering questions over real-world documents requires processing long inputs that interleave text with tables. Optical context compression, which represents context as images, promises to reduce token cost, but its effect on table understanding remains unclear. We study pixel-level table compression for question answering over documents with multiple tables, evaluating seven VLMs across two benchmarks and five visual-token budgets. At moderate budgets, table images match html in accuracy with fewer tokens, but aggressive downscaling makes models reason longer without recovering accuracy, eroding the savings. Yet even at 64 visual tokens per table, tables preserve enough signal to identify whether they are relevant to a question. We exploit this asymmetry with a training-free, two-stage method: the model first identifies the tables needed to answer a question from a pixel-compressed context, and then reasons over those tables at native resolution. On long financial documents, it uses 41% fewer tokens than single-step QA over native-resolution tables while gaining 5 accuracy points, and 21% fewer than the most efficient compressed configuration at no accuracy cost. It also still saves tokens when applied to retrieved context.

items.title: Does Latent Planning Survive Point Clouds? Action-Conditioned JEPA World Models for Geometric Observations and Goals
items.summary: arXiv:2608.29434v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Latent action world models let agents plan new behaviors at test time by predicting how actions change the environment, and joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) do so by forecasting future latent states rather than pixels. Yet nearly all such models see the world through a camera, even though robotic manipulation is fundamentally geometric: in robotics goals for manipulation are traditionally specified by target object poses, not by images of the object once placed. We ask whether latent planning survives a shift from appearance to geometry, on the observation side as well as on the goal specifications side. To answer this, we extend the stable-worldmodel evaluation platform with simulated LiDAR-style raycast point clouds as a new sensor modality, and adapt three JEPA designs to point clouds: a frozen-encoder model built on Utonia features, a distribution-prior model based on LeWM, and an action-sensitive model based on Delta-JEPA. We further introduce a goal-encoding mechanism that constructs the goal latent from the current latent and a 3D target pose, removing the need for goal images or goal point clouds. A comparative evaluation of the different anti-collapse mechanisms shows that point-cloud world models can match their image-based counterparts, demonstrating that the modality shift from appearance to geometry is achievable. All models are released as open weights with open-source training and inference code, to make world-model planning accessible for LiDAR-driven and pose-directed robotic tasks.

items.title: CRAD: Class-wise Reliability-Aware Distillation for Decentralized Heterogeneous Federated Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2609.00446v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Conventional federated learning (FL) relies on parameter averaging, which forces clients to be doubly homogeneous: it demands an identical architecture and degrades under non-IID data. Real-world deployments usually break both assumptions. We sidestep both by building a decentralized knowledge distillation framework in which each client evaluates its peers' model snapshots on its own local data and distills from the resulting soft predictions. Because knowledge is transferred through the shared class posterior, clients are free to run different architectures; and because every teacher is evaluated on the student's own device, raw data never leaves the client, with no central server or public dataset required. Within this setting, we identify and address an under-examined problem: how to combine the peer teacher predictions. Existing methods, like uniform averaging, ignore how knowledge reliability varies across teachers and classes. We propose Class-wise Reliability-Aware Distillation (CRAD), which, per class, first discards teachers that disagree with the peer consensus and then takes a weighted average of the rest, weighting each teacher by its per-class reliability (precision, or inverse variance). Since the variance of an accuracy from $n$ samples scales as $1/n$, support enters automatically: among the teachers that survive filtering, a teacher is trusted for a class to the degree that it is both accurate and well-evidenced for it. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and PathMNIST, across heterogeneous architectures under severe non-IID skew, CRAD consistently outperforms competing methods in global accuracy. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/bbilbeis/CRAD.

items.title: Untangling the Mechanisms of Misleading Context in Medical Question Answering
items.summary: arXiv:2609.02754v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models now answer medical questions with expert-level performance. However, the context these systems act on can be misleading, and misleading context can corrupt a model's medical judgment. To understand how misleading context corrupts this judgment, we examine the model's susceptibility to the context, disclosure of it, mechanism of corrupted reasoning, and monitorability of the decision. On the medical reasoning subset of MedMisBench, a clinician-reviewed question-answering benchmark of 8,627 questions, we inject two types of misleading context cues, fabricated evidence and a bare assertion. We test three reasoning models, two that expose their full reasoning trace and one frontier model that exposes only its response. All three are more susceptible to the assertion than to the fabricated evidence, adopting the asserted answer 10 to 27 points more often. The misleading cues are disclosed in 81 to 98% of traces but only 7 to 90% of responses, and the assertion is disclosed less often than evidence based cues. Resampling from reasoning traces without disclosure shows the two cues corrupt reasoning differently, evidence entering early and accumulating while the assertion redirects the conclusion near its end. An LLM monitor catches 78% of corrupted decisions at 5% false positives when reading an open model's trace with guidance, against at most 32% from any response. The misleading context that models are most susceptible to is disclosed least, and was caught reliably only from an open reasoning trace, which frontier providers withhold.

items.title: Do Latent World Models Really Select the Right Actions?
items.summary: arXiv:2609.05461v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper shows that the planning success of a latent world model does not reveal how well its score selects actions. Latent world models score candidate action sequences by the distance between their predicted embeddings and the embedding of a goal image, and their strong planning results are naturally read as evidence that this score picks good actions. Our study is simple: we take two released models, JEPA-WM and DINO-WM, execute the action sequences their planners consider, and compare what the score prefers with what actually happens. We make two observations. First, the score is informative but unreliable: it picks better actions than chance, yet it often passes over a successful sequence that the search has already found. Second, planning still succeeds, helped by a wider search and by replanning from new observations. With the released search budget, PointMaze planning succeeds in 91% of episodes, yet the top-scored candidate at the end of a search is no more likely to succeed than a random one. These observations suggest that the score should be measured directly, next to the success rate.

items.title: From Synthetic Priors to Model Behavior: Structural Coverage in Tabular Foundation Models
items.summary: arXiv:2609.06912v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are commonly pretrained on large collections of procedurally generated synthetic tasks, yet it remains unclear how well these synthetic pretraining priors support the downstream tasks on which the models are evaluated. We study this from a distribution-level attribution perspective. We recover or reconstruct the synthetic data generators of four TFMs and compare their generated tasks with datasets from two widely used tabular benchmarks. Each dataset is represented by a common set of structural descriptors capturing schema, feature distributions, dependence structure, response properties, and feature--response relationships. We then measure how broadly and repeatedly each synthetic prior reaches benchmark tasks using structural coverage and normalized density, and examine whether stronger local support is associated with better predictive performance. We find substantial differences across synthetic pretraining priors: some generators provide broader and denser support for benchmark tasks than others. Moreover, stronger synthetic-to-benchmark support is generally associated with better relative model performance, although this association is largely driven by the model with the broadest support and mostly disappears once each model's average support is removed. These results suggest that structural coverage provides a useful diagnostic for characterizing synthetic pretraining priors, whereas its relationship to downstream model behavior mainly reflects differences between models and remains confounded with architecture and training.

items.title: Constrained Online Learning with Noisy Constraint Values
items.summary: arXiv:2609.06921v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study online convex optimization with time-varying constraints when the constraint values are observed only through noise. In each round the learner picks an action, pays a convex loss, and incurs a convex constraint value that should be nonpositive; it then receives unbiased estimates of the loss and constraint gradients, and an unbiased observation of the constraint value whose error has bounded variance. Performance is measured against the best fixed action in hindsight among those that satisfy every constraint, and violation by the largest total overspend over any interval of consecutive rounds, which we call budget violation. Our algorithm, LEDGER, has $O(\sqrt T)$ expected regret and $O(\sqrt{T\log T})$ expected budget violation over $T$ rounds, uses one projection per round, and needs no strictly feasible action. items.title: Support Topology and Gradient Mixing in Sinkhorn Layers
items.summary: arXiv:2609.07954v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sinkhorn attention layers normalize weights over a fixed sparse mask by alternating row and column scaling. When training these layers, sparse masks are usually judged by their edge count, graph diameter, or forward reachability. We show that the sparsity pattern and marginal budgets also govern how gradients flow backward through the scaling steps. Differentiating one row-column cycle on column log-potentials yields an explicit row-stochastic Markov kernel built from the two half-step transport plans, which reduces to a reversible two-step random walk at a balanced fixed point. Because potentials are defined only up to additive constants on each connected component, reverse-mode gradients propagate as zero-sum vectors whose total-variation norm contracts at a rate given by the kernel's Dobrushin coefficient. This coefficient bounds both unrolled backpropagation and implicit-differentiation truncation error. Crucially, graph connectivity alone does not prevent gradient trapping: we prove a face-lattice dichotomy showing that a mask and marginals guarantee score-uniform one-step contraction if and only if every nonempty face of the transportation polytope retains pairwise two-hop column overlap; otherwise, large learned scores can push the contraction rate arbitrarily close to one. We extend this criterion to multi-layer schedules, prove exact one-sweep mixing for coordinate-factorized and butterfly masks, and derive closed-form bounds for expanders, local bands, and global hub tokens. Deterministic numerical checks verify our finite-difference adjoints, canonical sparse masks, adversarial score limits, and spectral formulas.

items.title: Fairness Auditing After Model Updating: Reliability of Paired Disparity Comparisons
items.summary: arXiv:2609.09788v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Model updates can change disparities in prediction errors between demographic groups. We examine whether retrospective audits can reliably assess these changes by comparing updated models with their unchanged initial models on the same independent labelled observations, holding completed updating histories fixed. The target is the updated-minus-frozen difference in absolute subgroup gaps, averaged equally across reporting periods and assessed separately for true-positive and false-positive rates. Exploratory controlled simulations and repeated audits of fixed simulated histories assess coverage and decision correctness for nominal 95% intervals. Across the broader history panel, changing interval construction can raise or lower estimated coverage. In one subgroup-drift setting, 2,000 true-positive-rate audits evaluated twenty selected histories updated at fixed intervals, using 1,250 observations per reporting period. Replacing percentile bootstrap intervals with full-size basic intervals reduced estimated coverage from 92.20% to 84.55%. At an illustrative margin of 0.5 percentage points, correct conclusive decisions increased from 78 to 376, while incorrect decisions increased from 3 to 43, including 13 false reductions. The constructions used identical observations, estimates and bootstrap draws and had equal widths. Other controlled examples frequently excluded the population change while correctly indicating an increase. More conclusive audit results therefore need not provide more reliable evidence. Claims that updating reduced disparity require an inference procedure justified for the target and sampling design, an explicit decision margin, and group-specific performance reporting.
