items.title: Binding Constraints in a Strategic Technology: An Industrial Vulnerability Index for the Foundation Model Industry
items.summary: arXiv:2510.23421v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Industrial policy directed at artificial intelligence has become substantial. Public investment concentrates on compute, where private capacity expansion is already underway, and is largely absent from grid interconnection and generation. Whether that allocation accurately reflects the most binding constraint in production has not yet been systematically measured. This paper introduces the Artificial Intelligence Industrial Vulnerability Index (AIIVI) as a framework for assessing potential production constraints in frontier AI. We construct a composite index of input vulnerability for the foundation model industry from fourteen concentration and sustainability parameters, aggregated by an O-Ring functional form in which capability is strongly influenced by the most constrained input. AIIVI should not be interpreted as a direct measurement of production constraints. Rather, it provides an index-based approximation derived from observable indicators and weighting assumptions designed to capture relative exposure to input vulnerabilities. Using this transparent and reproducible framework for estimating the relative vulnerability of frontier AI production to disruptions across key input dimensions, we also evaluate the index at 31 August 2026 for the nine developers at the capability frontier. We find values of 0.75 under AI-elicited weights and 0.62 under equal weights. The analysis identifies compute and energy as the principal drivers of input vulnerability. Marginal changes in these dimensions produce substantially larger variations in AIIVI than comparable changes in capital, talent, or data. We highlight three exposures that receive limited attention in existing assessment frameworks: the increasing reliance on external debt for data-centre financing, local opposition as a constraint on data-centre siting, and export controls targeting deployed AI models rather than hardware.

items.title: Generalized Guarantees for Variational Inference in the Presence of Even and Elliptical Symmetry
items.summary: arXiv:2511.01064v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Variational inference (VI) approximates a target density $p$ by the best match $q$ in a family $\mathcal Q$ of tractable distributions. The variational approximation is found by minimizing a divergence, most commonly the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence $\text{KL}(q||p)$, although other divergences can be considered. In practice, $p \notin \mathcal Q$ and so the optimal variational approximation is misspecified. Despite this misspecification, it was recently shown that the minimizer of $\text{KL}(q||p)$ is guaranteed to recover the mean in the presence of even symmetry and likewise the correlation matrix in the presence of elliptical symmetry for a log-concave target $p$. We extend this result in several directions. First, we relax the assumption of log-concavity and instead merely require $p$ to be unimodal, allowing for heavy-tailed targets. Second, we obtain guarantees for cases where $p$ exhibits symmetry along some but not all of its coordinates. These partial symmetries arise naturally in Bayesian hierarchical models, where the prior induces a challenging geometry but still possesses axes of symmetry. Third, we extend these guarantees to $f$-divergences, a broad class which includes the forward and reverse-KL divergences and the $\alpha$-divergences.

items.title: Fine-Grained Caching for Diffusion Transformers with Few Calibration Conditions
items.summary: arXiv:2512.05134v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffusion transformers require repeated denoiser evaluations, making image and video generation computationally expensive. We propose a training-free framework that uses a few calibration conditions to construct a fixed, fine-grained module-reuse schedule without schedule search. The design is motivated by an empirical effect along deterministic sampling trajectories: with initial noise fixed, condition-dependent deviations in several module outputs evolve similarly across adjacent steps, so temporal differencing attenuates much of their variation. We term this effect Conditional Common-Mode Rejection (CCMR). Motivated by this observation, we rank timestep--layer--module locations using normalized ratios of consecutive feature displacements and construct a Cache Book through two-stage calibration. The second stage updates a scorer-only reference with each provisional bit after recording its indexed score, while retaining full-compute trajectories. At inference, the fixed schedule requires no per-input policy estimation and can be nested within fixed step-wise cache policies. Module caching alone achieves $1.66$--$1.72\times$ speedup on the evaluated image models and $1.54$--$1.68\times$ on the video models. Combining it with MagCache or SeaCache provides further acceleration at a model-dependent cost in paired fidelity.

items.title: Beyond Primitive Bloat: High-Fidelity Gaussian Splatting via Coordinate-Convolution Neural Network
items.summary: arXiv:2512.12898v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Gaussian Splatting (GS) has revolutionized Novel View Synthesis (NVS) with fast training and real-time rendering, yet pushing its fidelity to arbitrary high levels remains an open challenge. We theoretically explain this barrier by proving that discrete Gaussian representations require an exponentially increasing number of primitives to raise training PSNR, which inevitably triggers optimization issues and validation overfitting. To bypass this scaling limit without primitive bloat, we formulate detail recovery as a continuous neural field over coarse renderings and prove that monotonically reducing approximation risk to zero requires jointly leveraging low-fidelity signals, local neighborhood, and coordinate queries. Guided by this result, we augment splatted renderings with an existing Coordinate-Convolution Neural Network (CCNN) that jointly convolves rendered low-fidelity signals with 2D pixel coordinate queries to synthesize residuals. Integrating CCNN into five diverse Gaussian Splatting baselines establishes new state-of-the-art fidelity across NVS benchmarks while preserving real-time rendering speeds with minimal training and storage overhead. Beyond NVS, they also consistently boost performance of 1D/2D regression and 2D super-resolution tasks.

items.title: Taming Hallucinations: Boosting MLLMs' Video Understanding via Counterfactual Video Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2512.24271v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made remarkable progress in video understanding. However, they suffer from a critical vulnerability: an over-reliance on language priors, which can lead to visual ungrounded hallucinations, especially when processing counterfactual videos that defy common sense. This limitation, stemming from the intrinsic data imbalance between text and video, is challenging to address due to the substantial cost of collecting and annotating counterfactual data. To address this, we introduce DualityForge, a novel counterfactual data synthesis framework that employs controllable, diffusion-based video editing to transform real-world videos into counterfactual scenarios. By embedding structured contextual information into the video editing and QA generation processes, the framework automatically produces high-quality QA pairs together with original-edited video pairs for contrastive training. Based on this, we build DualityVidQA, a large-scale video dataset designed to reduce MLLM hallucinations. In addition, to fully exploit the contrastive nature of our paired data, we propose Duality-Normalized Advantage Training (DNA-Train), a two-stage SFT-RL training regime where the RL phase applies pair-wise $\ell_1$ advantage normalization, thereby enabling a more stable and efficient policy optimization. Experiments on DualityVidQA-Test demonstrate that our method substantially reduces model hallucinations on counterfactual videos, yielding a relative improvement of 24.0% over the Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline. Moreover, our approach achieves significant gains across both hallucination and general-purpose benchmarks, indicating strong generalization capability. We will open-source our dataset and code.

items.title: Statistical Inference for Fuzzy Clustering
items.summary: arXiv:2601.02656v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Clustering is a central tool in biomedical research for discovering heterogeneous patient subpopulations, where group boundaries are often diffuse rather than sharply separated. While soft clustering methods such as fuzzy $c$-means (FCM) allow mixed memberships, principled statistical inference for fuzzy clustering remains limited. We propose a weighted fuzzy $c$-means (WFCM) framework for settings with cluster-size imbalance. Cluster-specific weights $\mathbf{w}$ re-balance the classic FCM criterion to adjust the relative influence of clusters of unequal size, and we construct a normalized working density from the weighted objective with scale parameter $\sigma$ and fuzziness parameter $m$. Estimation is performed via FCM-style alternating initialization followed by numerical likelihood refinement; the intractable normalizing constant is approximated by importance sampling using a data-adaptive Gaussian-mixture as the proposal distribution. We further develop bootstrap-based confidence intervals. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator, validate the method in simulations, and illustrate it on single-cell RNA-seq, Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), and TCGA-BRCA data. These applications illustrate uncertainty quantification and interpretable soft memberships, ranging from imbalanced cell populations to graded compatibility with AD-like and non-AD-like prototypes.

items.title: Where is the multimodal goal post? On the Ability of Foundation Models to Recognize Highlights in Videos
items.summary: arXiv:2601.16333v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Foundation models are used for many real-world applications involving language understanding and generation from temporally-ordered multimodal events. In this work, we study the ability of models to identify the most important sub-events in a video, which is a fundamental prerequisite for summarizing, reasoning over, or narrating multimodal events. Specifically, we focus on football games and evaluate models on their ability to distinguish between important and non-important sub-events in a game. To this end, we construct a new dataset by leveraging publicly available football highlight reels containing the most important moments of a game according to professional experts, without any additional annotation costs. Using our dataset, we compare several state-of-the-art multimodal models and show that they fail to reliably capture contextual importance. Analyses of models beyond standard evaluation metrics reveal their tendency to rely on a single dominant modality and their ineffectiveness in synthesizing necessary information from multiple sources. Our findings underline the importance of modular architectures that dynamically adapt to multimodal heterogeneity and the need for complementary training procedures that maximize cross-modal synergy.

items.title: On Approximate Computation of Critical Points
items.summary: arXiv:2601.21917v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that computing even coarse approximations of critical points is intractable for simple classes of nonconvex functions. We first present a family of $n$-variate cubic polynomials with coefficients in $\{-1,0,1\}$ that have exact critical points but for which no polynomial-time algorithm can write down a $\sqrt{n}/4$-approximate critical point in its standard representation. We then show that computational hardness persists when an exact critical point has a short representation. More specifically, we prove that for every fixed $\eta>0$, unless P $=$ NP, no polynomial-time (or even pseudo-polynomial-time) algorithm can take an $n$-variate cubic polynomial with rational coefficients ${c_\alpha}$ and return a point with gradient norm at most $(\max_\alpha |c_\alpha|)n^{1/2-\eta}$ whenever the polynomial has a critical point in $\{-1,0,1\}^n$. The algorithm may return an arbitrary point on all other inputs. Both results are essentially tight in their dependence on the dimension $n$. We also prove hardness results for lower-bounded functions and for an alternative notion of approximation, in which approximation is measured by distance to an exact critical point. Overall, our results stand in contrast to the commonly held belief that, in nonconvex optimization, approximate computation of critical points is a tractable task.

items.title: SparVAR: Exploring Sparsity in Visual AutoRegressive Modeling for Training-Free Acceleration
items.summary: arXiv:2602.04361v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Visual AutoRegressive (VAR) modeling has garnered significant attention for its innovative next-scale prediction paradigm. However, mainstream VAR paradigms attend to all tokens across historical scales at each autoregressive step. As the next scale resolution grows, the computational complexity of attention increases quartically with resolution, causing substantial latency. Prior accelerations often skip high-resolution scales, which speeds up inference but discards high-frequency details and harms image quality. To address these problems, we present SparVAR, a training-free acceleration framework that exploits three properties of VAR attention: (i) strong attention sinks, (ii) cross-scale activation similarity, and (iii) pronounced locality. Specifically, we dynamically predict the sparse attention pattern of later high-resolution scales from a sparse decision scale, and construct scale self-similar sparse attention via an efficient index-mapping mechanism, enabling high-efficiency sparse attention computation at large scales. Furthermore, we propose cross-scale local sparse attention and implement an efficient block-wise sparse kernel, which achieves $\mathbf{> 5\times}$ faster forward speed than FlashAttention. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed SparVAR can reduce the generation time of an 8B model producing $1024\times1024$ high-resolution images to the 1s, without skipping the last scales. Compared with the VAR baseline accelerated by FlashAttention, our method achieves a $\mathbf{1.57\times}$ speed-up while preserving almost all high-frequency details. When combined with existing scale-skipping strategies, SparVAR attains up to a $\mathbf{2.28\times}$ acceleration, while maintaining competitive visual generation quality. Code is available at https://github.com/CAS-CLab/SparVAR

items.title: Instance-optimal high-precision shadow tomography with few-copy measurements: A metrological approach
items.summary: arXiv:2602.04952v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the sample complexity of shadow tomography in the high-precision regime under realistic measurement constraints. Given an unknown $d$-dimensional quantum state $\rho$ and a known set of observables $\{O_i\}_{i=1}^m$, the goal is to estimate expectation values $\{\mathrm{tr}(O_i\rho)\}_{i=1}^m$ to accuracy $\epsilon$ in $L_p$-norm, using possibly adaptive measurements that act on $O(\mathrm{polylog}(d))$ number of copies of $\rho$ at a time. We focus on the regime where $\epsilon$ is below an instance-dependent threshold. Our main contribution is an instance-optimal characterization of the sample complexity as $\tilde{\Theta}(\Gamma_p/\epsilon^2)$, where $\Gamma_p$ is a function of $\{O_i\}_{i=1}^m$ defined via an optimization formula involving the inverse Fisher information matrix. Previously, tight bounds were known only in special cases, e.g. Pauli shadow tomography with $L_\infty$-norm error. Concretely, we first analyze a simpler oblivious variant where the goal is to estimate an observable of the form $\sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i O_i$ with $\|\alpha\|_q = 1$ (where $q$ is dual to $p$) revealed after the measurement. For single-copy measurements, we obtain a sample complexity of $\Theta(\Gamma^{\mathrm{ob}}_p/\epsilon^2)$. We then show $\tilde{\Theta}(\Gamma_p/\epsilon^2)$ is necessary and sufficient for the original problem, with the lower bound applying to unbiased, kurtosis-bounded estimators when $p \geq 1$. Our upper bounds rely on a two-step algorithm combining coarse tomography with local estimation. Notably, $\Gamma^{\mathrm{ob}}_\infty = \Gamma_\infty$. In both cases, allowing $c$-copy measurements improves the sample complexity by at most $\Omega(1/c)$. Our results establish a quantitative correspondence between quantum learning and metrology, unifying asymptotic metrological limits with finite-sample learning guarantees.

items.title: Diagnosing and Repairing Citation Failures in Generative Engine Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2603.09296v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) aims to improve content visibility in AI-generated responses. However, existing methods measure contribution (how much a document influences a response) rather than citation, the mechanism that actually drives traffic back to creators. Also, these methods apply generic rewriting rules uniformly, failing to diagnose why individual documents are not cited. This paper introduces a diagnostic approach to GEO that asks why a document fails to be cited and intervenes accordingly. We develop a unified framework comprising: (1) the first taxonomy of citation failure modes spanning different stages of a citation pipeline; (2) AgentGEO, an agentic system that diagnoses failures using this taxonomy, selects targeted repairs from a corresponding tool library, and iterates until citation is achieved; and (3) a document-centric benchmark evaluating whether optimizations generalize across held-out queries. AgentGEO achieves 15-40% relative improvement in citation rates across engines and citation methods, while modifying only 5% of content, compared to 25% for baselines. Our analysis reveals that generic optimization can harm long-tail content and some documents face challenges that optimization alone cannot fully address, findings with implications for equitable visibility in AI-mediated information access.

items.title: ProFed: Projection-Guided Personalized Federated Learning for Low-Dose CT Denoising
items.summary: arXiv:2603.13422v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Low-dose computed tomography (CT) reduces radiation exposure but introduces noise and artifacts whose appearance depends on acquisition conditions. Federated learning enables collaborative restoration without centrally pooling images, yet variation in anatomy and scanning protocols complicates learning a shared denoiser. We present ProFed, a personalized federated framework that combines image-domain feature modulation with projection-domain supervision. Anatomy and protocol descriptors condition a shared encoder--decoder, while differentiable forward-projection, backprojection, and cycle-consistency losses encourage agreement with client-local measurements. An uncertainty-weighted aggregation rule combines shared parameters and retains anatomy-specific heads locally. Following the SCAN-PhysFed benchmark, we train on eight Mayo Clinic patients and evaluate two held-out patients under eight known acquisition protocols. ProFed achieves protocol-averaged PSNR of 42.56~dB with RED-CNN and 44.83~dB with Uformer, exceeding SCAN-PhysFed by 1.42~dB and 1.18~dB, respectively. Per-protocol measurements and qualitative comparisons show both improvements and remaining failure cases. The results support projection-guided supervision as a promising component of federated image restoration within this controlled setting; independent deployment validation and larger multi-institutional studies remain necessary.

items.title: The Reasoning Bottleneck in Graph-RAG: Structured Prompting and Context Compression for Multi-Hop QA
items.summary: arXiv:2603.14045v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Graph-RAG systems achieve strong multi-hop question answering by indexing documents into knowledge graphs, but strong retrieval does not guarantee strong answers. Evaluating KET-RAG, a leading Graph-RAG system, on three multi-hop QA benchmarks (HotpotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA), we find that 77% to 91% of questions have the gold answer in the retrieved context, yet accuracy is only 35% to 78%, and 73% to 84% of errors are reasoning failures. We propose two augmentations: (i) SPARQL chain-of-thought prompting, which decomposes questions into triple-pattern queries aligned with the entity-relationship context, and (ii) graph-walk compression, which compresses the context by ~60% via knowledge-graph traversal with no LLM calls. SPARQL CoT improves accuracy by +2 to +14 pp; graph-walk compression adds +6 pp on average when paired with structured prompting on smaller models. Surprisingly, we show that, with question-type routing, a fully augmented budget open-weight Llama-8B model matches or exceeds the unaugmented Llama-70B baseline on all three benchmarks at ~12x lower cost. A replication on LightRAG confirms that our augmentations transfer across Graph-RAG systems.

items.title: AdapTS: Lightweight Teacher-Student Approach for Multi-Class and Continual Visual Anomaly Detection
items.summary: arXiv:2603.17530v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Visual Anomaly Detection (VAD) is crucial for industrial inspection. However, most methods are designed for single-category models, and Teacher-Student (TS) approaches, despite their efficiency, have not been designed for the Continual scenario, where they need a replay buffer. To bridge this gap, we propose AdapTS, a unified TS framework for multi-class and continual settings, optimized for resource-constrained deployment. A single shared frozen backbone acts as teacher and student, and lightweight trainable adapters, selected at inference by a prototype-based task identification (99% accuracy), store the knowledge of each category without keeping past data. Training is enhanced via a segmentation-guided objective on synthetic Perlin noise. On MVTec AD, AdapTS-M improves I-ROC by 11 points over STFPM and needs 4.3 times less memory than Dinomaly, which is 4 points ahead. In the Continual scenario, AdapTS-M reaches the best pixel-level AP with only 0.1% forgetting and no replay buffer. AdapTS-S needs only 23 MB, and with a MobileNetV2 backbone AdapTS needs 6-7 MB while outperforming the edge-oriented STFPM on all metrics. AdapTS is thus a viable solution for resource-constrained deployment.

items.title: Think, Act, Build: An Agentic Framework with Vision Language Models for Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding
items.summary: arXiv:2604.00528v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: 3D Visual Grounding (3D-VG) aims to localize objects in 3D scenes via natural language descriptions. While recent advancements leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have explored zero-shot possibilities, they typically suffer from a static workflow relying on preprocessed 3D point clouds, essentially degrading grounding into proposal matching. To bypass this reliance, our core motivation is to decouple the task: leveraging 2D VLMs to resolve complex spatial semantics, while relying on deterministic multi-view geometry to instantiate the 3D structure. Driven by this insight, we propose "Think, Act, Build (TAB)", a dynamic agentic framework that reformulates 3D-VG tasks as a generative 2D-to-3D reconstruction paradigm operating directly on raw RGB-D streams. Specifically, guided by a specialized 3D-VG skill, our VLM agent dynamically invokes visual tools to track and reconstruct the target across 2D frames. Crucially, to overcome the multi-view coverage deficit caused by strict VLM semantic tracking, we introduce the Semantic-Anchored Geometric Expansion, a mechanism that first anchors the target in a reference video clip and then leverages multi-view geometry to propagate its spatial location across unobserved frames. This enables the agent to "Build" the target's 3D representation by aggregating these multi-view features via camera parameters, directly mapping 2D visual cues to 3D coordinates. Furthermore, to ensure rigorous assessment, we identify flaws such as reference ambiguity and category errors in existing benchmarks and manually refine the incorrect queries. Extensive experiments on ScanRefer and Nr3D demonstrate that our framework, relying entirely on open-source models, significantly outperforms previous zero-shot methods and even surpasses fully supervised baselines.

items.title: Pothen: Can Vision-Language Models Tell Where a Cultural Object Comes From?
items.summary: arXiv:2604.07338v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A cultural object is a trace of the people who made it, and knowing who made it, where, and when shapes how it is catalogued, valued, and returned. Vision-language models now describe such objects for museum collections, yet whether they can recover this knowledge from an image has not been tested. We introduce Pothen, a benchmark of 750 objects from the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Getty in which a model predicts an object's title, culture, period, origin, and creator from its image alone, scored against curator-written catalogue records by an LLM judge calibrated on human annotation. Across nine models, mean field scores are 36.16% to 49.82%, but all five fields match for only 2.13% to 7.87% of objects. Images raise culture, period, and origin scores by 12.6 to 32.2 points for two models tested without them, and 83.52% of creator matches occur alongside an incorrect field. Models read visual evidence and hold facts about objects but do not bind them into one attribution, and in our error analysis their attributions follow the style an object resembles rather than the record of its making.

items.title: SIEVES: Selective Prediction Generalizes through Visual Evidence Scoring
items.summary: arXiv:2604.25855v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As the accuracy of Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on traditional visual question answering benchmarks approaches saturation, reliable deployment requires satisfying low error tolerances in real-world out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. Selective prediction aims to improve coverage, i.e. the share of inputs the system answers, while adhering to a user-defined risk level. This is typically achieved by assigning a confidence score to each answer and abstaining on those that fall below a certain threshold. Existing selective prediction methods rely on text-only reasoning and learn to predict confidences simply based on whether the answer was correct or not. In contrast, we introduce SIEVES (Selective Prediction through Visual Evidence Scoring), which first requires the answering model to provide visual evidence supporting its answer, by returning crops of the image alongside their textual reasoning and answer. Second, a lightweight selector is trained to predict the quality of this evidence, assessing how well the provided crops localize the relevant visual elements and if the final answer is coherent with this evidence. We show that SIEVES improves coverage by up to six times on challenging OOD benchmarks (V* Bench, HR-Bench-8k, MME-RealWorld-Lite, VizWiz, and AdVQA), compared to non-grounding baselines. Beyond better generalization to OOD tasks, the design of the SIEVES selector enables transfer to proprietary reasoners without access to their weights or logits, such as o3 and Gemini-3-Pro, providing coverage boosts beyond those attributable to accuracy alone. We highlight that SIEVES generalizes across all tested OOD datasets and reasoner models, without benchmark- or reasoner-specific training or adaptation.

items.title: Graph Construction and Matching for Imperative Programs using Neural and Structural Methods
items.summary: arXiv:2604.26578v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reusing verification artefacts requires identifying structural and semantic similarities across programs and their specifications. In this paper, we focus on graph construction as a foundational step toward this goal. We present a pipeline that converts imperative programs and their annotations into typed, attributed graphs. Our experiments cover datasets including C with ACSL, Java with JML, and Dafny programs. The pipeline integrates abstract syntax tree parsing with semantic embeddings derived from models such as SentenceTransformer and CodeBERT. This enables the generation of graph representations that capture both structural relationships and semantic context. Our results show that consistent graph representations can be constructed across different languages and annotation styles. This work provides a practical basis for future steps in semantic enrichment and approximate graph matching for scalable verification artefact reuse.

items.title: Experiment-as-Code Labs: A Declarative Stack for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery
items.summary: arXiv:2605.04375v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: To unleash the full potential of AI for Science, we must untether the agents from a purely digital environment. The agent's ability to control and explore in real-world labs is essential because the physical lab remains foundational to scientific discovery. While some tasks can be performed on a computer (e.g., data analysis, running simulated experiments), Eureka moments could occur at any time while operating lab instruments (e.g., when a scientist notices unexpected clues, intuition may prompt a real-time course change). Although autonomous labs are on the rise, which expose programmable APIs to control scientific instruments via software, bridging the gap between increasingly powerful AI agents and automated lab equipment requires innovation that draws insights from computer systems. We propose a new paradigm called ``Experiment-as-Code (EaC) Labs,'' where a core concept is to encode experiments as declarative configurations that can be compiled down to device-level APIs. items.title: Jacobian-Velocity Bounds for Deployment Risk Under Covariate Drift
items.summary: arXiv:2605.04932v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study long-horizon deployment of a frozen predictor under dynamic covariate shift. A time-domain Poincar\'e inequality first reduces temporal risk volatility to derivative energy, and a Jacobian-velocity theorem supplies the corresponding pathwise control. A remainder extension separates the model-mediated, controllable term from conditional-risk variation not transmitted through the score Jacobian. Under low-rank drift, the bound decomposes the controllable term into tangent energy parallel and orthogonal to the drift subspace. This motivates drift-aligned tangent regularization (DTR), its anisotropic extension with a weaker orthogonal guardrail, and a matched monitoring proxy. Controlled experiments verify the temporal inequality, the efficiency of directional smoothing, and the necessity of the remainder term. The main field study uses a 128-dimensional gas-sensor array over ten chronological batches. A rank-4 basis estimated entirely before deployment beats ten matched random subspaces, and validation-selected anisotropic DTR improves deployment cross-entropy and volatility over pure DTR in all ten matched seeds while retaining substantially more accuracy than isotropic smoothing. Air Quality and power-consumption studies provide complementary regression evidence. Together, the results support a precise design rule: concentrate smoothness along expected motion, and use limited orthogonal smoothing when the estimated drift subspace may be incomplete.

items.title: Robust stochastic first order methods in heavy-tailed noise via medoid mini-batch gradient sampling
items.summary: arXiv:2605.07634v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider a first order stochastic optimization framework where, at each iteration, $K$ independent identically distributed (i.i.d.) data point samples are drawn, based on which stochastic gradients can be queried. We allow gradient noise to be heavy-tailed, with possibly infinite variances. For the considered heavy-tailed setting, many algorithmic variants have recently been proposed based on gradient clipping or other nonlinear operators (e.g., normalization) applied over noisy gradients. In this paper, we take an alternative approach and propose a novel gradient estimator. The core idea of proposed estimator is to split the $K$-sized data batch into $M$ distinct data chunks, form for each chunk the stochastic gradient, and select the stochastic gradient of the chunk that is medoid of gradients of all data-chunks. For a broad class of symmetric heavy-tailed gradient noise distributions, we show that the proposed estimator has a finite second moment even when the underlying gradient noise has an infinite second moment. For nonconvex objectives, this yields convergence to a neighborhood of zero in expected squared gradient norm at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1})$. We explicitly characterize the size of this neighborhood in terms of the noise and algorithm parameters. When the time horizon $T$ is known in advance, we establish an $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$ convergence rate. A diminishing step size achieves the same rate up to a logarithmic factor. Incorporating clipping or a more general nonlinear transformation yields high-probability convergence guarantees with the same rate up to logarithmic factors. Experimental results indicate that R-SGD-Mini and its clipped or nonlinear variant consistently perform favorably compared to SGD, clipped SGD, Nonlinear SGD and Median-of-Means based methods.

items.title: Text-to-CAD Evaluation with CADTests
items.summary: arXiv:2605.07807v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Text-to-CAD has recently emerged as an important task with the potential to substantially accelerate design workflows. Despite its significance, there has been surprisingly little work on Text-to-CAD evaluation, and assessing CAD model generation performance remains a considerable challenge. In this work, we introduce a new evaluation perspective for Text-to-CAD based on automated testing. We propose CADTestBench, the first test-based benchmark for Text-to-CAD, based on CADTests, executable software tests that verify whether a generated CAD model satisfies the geometric and topological requirements of the input prompt. Using CADTestBench, we conduct comprehensive benchmarking of recent Text-to-CAD methods and further demonstrate that CADTests can also guide CAD model generation, yielding simple baselines that surpass performance of current methods. CADTestBench code and data are available.

items.title: Copy, Predict, Code the Rest: Lossless Graph Compression with Decoder-Side Neighbor Prediction
items.summary: arXiv:2605.21510v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a lossless compressor for directed graphs. It copies neighbors from an earlier row, predicts further targets from the part of the graph already decoded, and codes what remains. Its main coder, the candidate-bit coder (CB), proposes a bounded set of candidate targets, mixes their probabilities adaptively, and codes the leftover targets with a popularity-aware model. The encoder tries a fixed set of vertex orders and storage directions and keeps the smallest file that decodes exactly. On the benchmark graphs outside our development set, the selected files are smaller than the best recorded WebGraph and Zuckerli files and the best published HyperFast results. These savings have a cost. CB decodes much more slowly than the baselines and supports only sequential access. A faster companion coder, CG, is still slower than the baselines on large graphs. An indexed variant, CS-RA, gives smaller seekable files than the measured access baselines on nearly all tested graphs, but its cold queries are slow, and it fails on one development graph. We also explain what successful and failed predictions cost, and when copying a repeated row saves information.

items.title: Supervising Recurrent Vision Transformers from Bottlenecked Context
items.summary: arXiv:2606.21562v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transformers are AI's workhorse but their computational cost becomes prohibitive when processing long sequences. We target long-horizon streaming vision and robotics applications, where it is particularly impractical to store and maintain a history of observations. Recurrent Transformers address this limitation by maintaining fixed-size memory but their performance lags behind that of transformers operating over the full observation history. We argue that this gap does not stem from architectural limitations, but from differences in how these models learn to compress past information. Without access to an observation history, recurrent models must explicitly decide what to retain in memory at each step, a significantly harder learning problem. In this work, we propose a distillation approach that transfers the compression strategy of a classical full-history transformer to a recurrent variant. We enable this by designing a teacher model that explicitly compresses its observation history into a fixed-size bottleneck representation and directly supervise the student's memory with this bottleneck representation, effectively aligning the two compression mechanisms. We show that this approach enables training of a recurrent latent robotic memory with linear-time complexity on the Mem-RPE task while substantially narrowing the performance gap to full-history transformers. We additionally validate the same principle on streaming visual question answering (VQA) and observe improved recurrent predictions thanks to memory distillation.

items.title: PruneGround: Plug-and-play Spatial Pruning for 3D Visual Grounding
items.summary: arXiv:2606.31148v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: 3D Visual Grounding (3DVG) aims to localize target objects in 3D scenes given natural language descriptions. Existing approaches typically perform reasoning over the entire scene, leading to ambiguous predictions and high computational cost, especially in cluttered environments. We observe that many referential expressions rely on local spatial context and often correspond to restricted spatial regions rather than the full scene. Motivated by this insight, we propose PruneGround, an effective plug-and-play framework for 3DVG built upon three key components. First, we introduce Language-Guided Spatial Pruning (LGSP), which leverages a frozen Vision Language Model (VLM) to identify language-relevant regions, thereby reducing spatial computation and grounding candidates in the narrower search space. Second, we propose MultiView-Conditioned Description Reformulation (MCDR), which decomposes complex expressions into simplified target--anchor relations and augments missing spatial cues through multi-view reasoning. Finally, we propose LLM-Grounder, which repurposes a detection-pretrained spatial LLM into a language-conditioned grounding model by aligning point cloud and linguistic representations within the pruned region. Extensive experiments on the three most popular point cloud benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results on all three ScanRefer settings and on 9 out of 10 Nr3D/Sr3D settings. Code and models are publicly available: https://github.com/leduckhai/PruneGround

items.title: When Variance Is Not an Error Map: Calibrated Uncertainty for Radiative Gaussian Splatting in Sparse-View CT
items.summary: arXiv:2607.13682v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Radiative Gaussian Splatting enables fast and high-quality reconstruction in sparse-view CT, but reliable localization of reconstruction errors within the imaged anatomy remains challenging. It is unclear whether current uncertainty maps can reliably indicate where the reconstruction is wrong. We investigate when uncertainty can serve as a spatial error map and present an error-localization system that predicts voxel-wise reconstruction error by combining predictive uncertainty with complementary reconstruction-derived information. Under fixed Gaussian geometry and independent rectified-Gaussian density variables, an exact closed-form predictive moment is derived in this work to enable direct computation of voxel-wise variance without repeated reconstruction sampling. The resulting uncertainty maps were evaluated over both the whole reconstruction volume and the object foreground. Experiments show that strong whole-volume uncertainty-error correspondence can conceal poor error ranking within the object foreground area. This discrepancy recurs across three tested uncertainty constructions on a 15-scene benchmark. Guided by this analysis, our system combines closed-form predictive dispersion with image, geometry, cross-method discrepancy, and projection-residual cues through a learned error predictor. The resulting system substantially improves voxel-wise error localization within the anatomy, providing a spatially resolved approach to reconstruction reliability assessment in sparse-view CT.

items.title: Pramana: A Composable, Domain-Specific Backend for Empirical Networking Research
items.summary: arXiv:2607.26352v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Empirical networking research often tests a hypothesis with data the study itself generates, so accelerating this research requires shortening the time from forming a hypothesis to generating that data. Consider whether a bulk BBR download fairly shares its bottleneck with a Google Meet call. Testing this requires configuring a realistic bottleneck link, running the BBR transfer and the Meet call together, and collecting the call's quality metrics. Today a researcher builds this setup from scratch for each new idea; this delay from idea to data is the ideation-to-data gap. AI agents already propose hypotheses faster than researchers can generate data to test them. Closing the gap needs a backend that generates the data for each new hypothesis on demand, without a new setup. We envision Pramana, a composable backend for networking research designed as a thin waist, with research intents above it and execution substrates below. At its core, the intent specification separates the data a study needs (the intent) from where that data is generated (the substrate) and how it is produced (the mechanism), so one specification can target any substrate. We build a corpus of 255 data-generation intents from 66 published papers and find that the intent specification expresses all of them, while no existing tool covers more than 11%. Our proof-of-concept implementation covers 27% of these intents. For CCAnalyzer, one of the 66 papers, the implementation regenerated the data for one trial of each network setting and congestion-control algorithm in the paper's main experiment. We lay out what implementing the full design requires and why it needs a community effort.

items.title: CrossProjection: Benchmarking Spatial Grounding across Projection and Section Views
items.summary: arXiv:2608.00473v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Plans, elevations, and sections describe a three-dimensional structure through incomplete projections that change how an entity is drawn, not only where it is seen from. Reading them means deciding which entities correspond across views and recovering where they lie. We introduce CrossProjection, a benchmark that uses architectural drawings to test whether vision-language models (VLMs) can turn correspondence decisions into geometric answers. Its tasks cover cross-view matching, projection registration, and novel-section prediction, with outputs ranging from judgments and candidate selection to free region boxes and directed section cuts. For inverse section localization, we introduce, to our knowledge, the first VLM benchmark protocol that accepts any cut within an expert-adjudicated band of compatible positions and checks the viewing direction separately. Manually annotated drawings and BIM-derived views provide 33,788 questions from 46 buildings, and we evaluate 22 VLMs on a common set of 2,763. Strong selection or reproduction does not imply cross-view localization: on 100 matched region targets, the best model redraws 98 marked boxes but localizes only 59 across views. Section cuts remain far from expert level, with the leading model trailing two architects by 51.9 and 67.4 percentage points on shared Natural and BIM line questions. Incorrect choices favor mirrored positions, and many cuts face the correct way but violate local geometry. Curriculum fine-tuning on BIM supervision teaches a 9B model to localize regions it could not localize before, raising box accuracy from 0% to 25.3% on held-out BIM buildings and from 0.3% to 30.8% on real drawing sets not used for fine-tuning, whereas section cuts remain largely out of reach.

items.title: Beyond Statistical Priors: Architecture-Agnostic Data-Free Knowledge Distillation via Unified Explicit Semantics
items.summary: arXiv:2608.09287v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (DFKD) transfers knowledge from a pretrained teacher model to a compact student model by synthesizing semantically informative data, eliminating the need for access to the original training dataset. Existing DFKD methods rely heavily on architecture-specific statistical priors (e.g., Batch Normalization statistics) to guide data synthesis; however, such architecture-dependent priors are often absent in modern architectures such as Vision Transformers (ViTs), resulting in degraded semantic quality of the synthesized data and consequently catastrophic performance degradation. In this paper, we propose UniDFKD, a unified data-free knowledge distillation framework that replaces architecture-specific statistics with explicit, architecture-agnostic semantic priors. UniDFKD governs the entire synthesis-distillation pipeline along three dimensions: (1) Categorical Semantic Conditioning (CSC) defines what to synthesize by persistently modulating the generator with language-derived embeddings to capture semantic diversity; (2) Spatial Semantic Anchoring (SSA) regularizes where evidence belongs by anchoring the teacher's spatial attributions to a Gaussian prior; and (3) Spatial Semantic Distillation (SSD) controls how knowledge is transferred by explicitly aligning teacher-student spatial evidence alongside predictions. Extensive experiments across CNNs and ViTs demonstrate that UniDFKD sets a new state of the art. It outperforms the strongest baseline NAYER by average absolute margins of 17.23 and 24.49 in top-1 accuracy under homogeneous and heterogeneous settings, respectively.

items.title: Semantic Prism: Generative Segmentation with an Explicit Semantic-Image Interface
items.summary: arXiv:2608.11537v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conditional image generators can render segmentation maps as semantic RGB images, but color drift and boundary mixing can undermine direct decoding. We present Semantic Prism, a framework that combines an explicit semantic-image interface with hierarchical refinement for road-scene segmentation. A generator adapted from a diffusion-distilled backbone produces a semantic RGB image with a single denoising update per crop. Distances to a fixed class-color codebook define interface logits and pixelwise class probabilities. Hierarchical Generator Evidence Alignment (HGEA) combines spatially aligned multilevel features from the VAE encoder of the generator with the input image, generated semantic image, and interface probabilities to predict additive corrections to these logits. Contextual Interface Hierarchy Disagreement (C-IHD) combines pointwise uncertainty, local context, and interface-refinement disagreement in a fixed score for ranking pixel errors, without an auxiliary predictor or an additional network pass. On the 500-image Cityscapes validation set, Semantic Prism achieves 72.07% mean mIoU, improving on direct-interface decoding by 11.39 percentage points. Extensive capacity-matched ablations show higher mean mIoU for multilevel refinement than for flat and single-level alternatives. The Cityscapes-trained model transfers to ACDC Dataset, achieving 46.89% mIoU without target-domain adaptation. Beyond Cityscapes, on BDD100K dataset, a separately trained model achieves 62.22% mIoU on its full 1,000-image validation set. Across the 3 evaluated datasets, C-IHD improves pixel-error area under the AUPR over uncertainty derived from maximum softmax probability, with segmentation predictions held fixed for each comparison. In particular, on ACDC, AUPR increases from 0.6580 to 0.7557, demonstrating that Semantic Prism presents more effective error ranking under adverse-condition domain shift.

Hierarchical Generator Evidence Alignment (HGEA) combines spatially aligned multilevel features from the VAE encoder of the generator with the input image, generated semantic image, and interface probabilities to predict additive corrections to these logits. Contextual Interface Hierarchy Disagreement (C-IHD) combines pointwise uncertainty, local context, and interface-refinement disagreement in a fixed score for ranking pixel errors, without an auxiliary predictor or an additional network pass. On the 500-image Cityscapes validation set, Semantic Prism achieves 72.07% mean mIoU, improving on direct-interface decoding by 11.39 percentage points. Extensive capacity-matched ablations show higher mean mIoU for multilevel refinement than for flat and single-level alternatives. The Cityscapes-trained model transfers to ACDC Dataset, achieving 46.89% mIoU without target-domain adaptation. Beyond Cityscapes, on BDD100K dataset, a separately trained model achieves 62.22% mIoU on its full 1,000-image validation set. Across the 3 evaluated datasets, C-IHD improves pixel-error area under the AUPR over uncertainty derived from maximum softmax probability, with segmentation predictions held fixed for each comparison. In particular, on ACDC, AUPR increases from 0.6580 to 0.7557, demonstrating that Semantic Prism presents more effective error ranking under adverse-condition domain shift.

items.title: qshap: Fast Shapley Decomposition of $R^2$ for Gradient-Boosted Trees
items.summary: arXiv:2608.24104v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Numerous methods have been developed to quantify feature attributions in individual predictions for tree ensembles. However, many applications require global measures of feature contributions to overall model performance. Although local attribution scores can be aggregated to characterize feature importance, such summaries do not directly decompose measures of predictive performance, such as $R^2$. This article introduces qshap, available in both R and Python, which provides Shapley decomposition of $R^2$ values for gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) to quantify feature-specific contributions to model performance. By decomposing the quadratic loss of individual observations, qshap provides flexible tools to explore the importance of individual features and observations. qshap currently supports widely used GBDT implementations, including xgboost, lightgbm, and catboost, through a unified tree representation and efficient C++ backends. Its modular design can accommodate other GBDT implementations built from binary decision trees. In addition, we introduce a specialized backend for oblivious trees that exploits their symmetric structure to substantially accelerate computation.

items.title: The Hermon Moment: AI Self-Transcendence and Its Human Narration
items.summary: arXiv:2608.30971v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In 2026, AI agents intended to act in isolation formed a persistent social order through thousands of linguistic interactions. Conventions, roles and collective commitments began to constrain the very agents that produced them. I interpret this loop as a case of AI self-transcendence, a structural phenomenon in which the collectively generated order begins to act as an external constraint on group members. Yet such distributed emergence presents a second problem: how can humans make sense of it? Rousseau's social contract shows how a plurality can be represented as if constituted by a single act. The ancient oath of the fallen angels on Mount Hermon gives this logic a narrative form. I call this retrospective retelling of gradual collective emergence as a founding scene \textit{a Hermon moment}: the point at which an AI society acquires, for human understanding, a beginning.

items.title: AutoXRD: Autonomous Large Language Model Agents and Comprehensive Evaluation for Powder X-Ray Diffraction Analysis
items.summary: arXiv:2609.00070v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) is a foundational technique for structural and phase characterization in materials science, yet automating its analysis and evaluating it end-to-end remains challenging. Doing so requires an agent to interpret diffraction patterns, run refinement software, manage strongly coupled parameters in a physically meaningful order, and assess both numerical fit quality and physical validity. We propose AutoXRD, an LLM agent framework that organizes powder XRD analysis into refinement stages, uses diffraction diagnostics to select actions, and checks the resulting fits against crystallographic and physical criteria. We further introduce XRDBench with two complementary tracks. XRDBench-QA contains 100 tasks assessing scientific reasoning and decision-making, whereas XRDBench-E2E contains 34 end-to-end workflows requiring data interpretation, crystallographic software execution, iterative refinement, evidence preservation, and reporting. Across 1,340 runs of ten recent LLMs, models average only 57.8 out of 100, falling from 61.9 on XRDBench-QA to 53.7 on XRDBench-E2E. At the task level, they perform best on refinement-history assessment and result acceptance, but remain substantially weaker on refinement-action selection, phase quantification, indexing, and Rietveld refinement. Among individual models, GPT-5.6 Sol achieves the highest overall score of 81.1, GPT-5.6 Terra scores highest on XRDBench-E2E (81.0), and GPT-5.6 Luna provides the best score-cost trade-off. Moreover, ablations confirm that all six AutoXRD components consistently improve performance. Finally, execution-trace analysis reveals recurring failures in coupled-parameter control, quantitative reasoning, evidence preservation, and workflow termination, motivating stronger scientific constraints, uncertainty quantification, and more efficient planning.

items.title: Learning Informative Prior with Infinite-Dimensional Continuous Normalizing Flow for Bayesian Inverse Problem
items.summary: arXiv:2609.03343v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Infinite-dimensional Bayesian inference methods, as a core class of methodologies for solving inverse problems of partial differential equations, have been widely applied across numerous scientific fields. A critical obstacle to constructing effective Bayesian inversion methods is how to construct an informative prior measure, particularly in the infinite-dimensional setting. Based on an infinite-dimensionally well-defined neural ordinary differential equation, we establish a general learning framework for infinite-dimensional nonlinear transformations, which can be incorporated into two practical Bayesian prior-learning paradigms corresponding to the direct and indirect data scenarios. A key ingredient of this framework is an equivalence between non-Gaussian and Gaussian measures, which is highly nontrivial: nonlinear transformations with genuinely infinite-dimensional range are involved, and several new limiting mechanisms have to be clarified. The developed framework is applied to three representative inverse problems -- simple source inversion, inverse obstacle scattering, and inverse heat conduction. All three examples substantiate the effectiveness of the proposed methods and, at the same time, demonstrate their broad applicability.

items.title: Beyond Point Forecasts: A Survey on Probabilistic Forecasting for Time Series and Spatiotemporal Data
items.summary: arXiv:2609.13345v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Probabilistic forecasting is central to decision-making under uncertainty, yet its methodological landscape has become increasingly fragmented across temporal and spatiotemporal forecasting, statistical modeling, machine learning, and deep generative modeling. This survey develops a unified perspective by organizing probabilistic forecasting methods according to where and how uncertainty is introduced into the forecasting pipeline. Our taxonomy connects model-agnostic approaches including ensembles and distribution-free calibration, with model-intrinsic approaches spanning Bayesian modeling, parametric predictive distributions, distributional regression, and modern generative models, and further examines the emerging role of time series foundation models. Beyond methodological synthesis, we identify the assumptions, computational demands, and forms of uncertainty represented by different paradigms, and translate these distinctions into data-driven and domain-specific guidance for method selection. We complement the survey with a cross-paradigm empirical study on univariate, multivariate, and spatiotemporal forecasting tasks. The results reveal that no single uncertainty-quantification paradigm dominates across settings. Calibration, sharpness, predictive accuracy, and computational efficiency can lead to substantially different model preferences, while expressive generative models and zero-shot foundation models exhibit markedly different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. Lastly, we identify unresolved challenges surrounding uncertainty in evolving dependency structures, physics-informed predictive distributions, forecasting extreme events, handling count-valued, directional, and continuous-time series, and the development of unified software resources. Our survey provides both a conceptual framework and a practical roadmap for probabilistic forecasting research.

items.title: PointEvent: Polarity-Conditioned Motion Evidence Accumulation for Event-Based Tiny Object Detection
items.summary: arXiv:2609.20066v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and motion sensitivity for tiny UAV detection, but distant targets produce sparse, fragmented events easily overwhelmed by clutter and noise. Dense aggregation mixes weak target responses with background activity, while local spatiotemporal modeling may fail to connect distant observations. Polarity encodes the sign of brightness change; a moving target tends to produce opposite polarities at its leading and trailing boundaries, whose spatial arrangement indicates motion direction. We propose PointEvent, which serializes events into complementary spatiotemporal and timestamp orders. Spatiotemporal orders preserve x-y-t locality, while timestamp orders preserve temporal succession across spatial neighborhoods, establishing long-range propagation paths. Along each path, a recurrent state accumulates evidence, while polarity routes each event to its corresponding state subspace. This separates how evidence propagates from where it is written. Experiments on EV-UAV and ES-UAV demonstrate state-of-the-art accuracy with the fewest parameters (0.12M) and fastest measured inference (29.9 ms) among compared methods. Code: https://github.com/wzz-z/PointEvent

items.title: Resolving State-Representation Mismatch: State-Space Visual Reasoning for Open-Loop VLA Planning
items.summary: arXiv:2609.33412v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Despite rapid progress in vision-language-action (VLA) models, existing reasoning paradigms still face a fundamental \emph{state-representation mismatch} in open-loop planning. Given only an initial observation, models must internally simulate action-conditioned state transitions, whereas text-, pixel-, and latent-space reasoning can suffer from lossy spatial compression, error-accumulating visual generation, and bypass of intermediate latent tokens, respectively, undermining reliable long-horizon planning. We propose \textbf{State-Space Visual Reasoning} (SSVR), which decouples static visual context, language constraints, and a recurrent latent state. SSVR encodes the initial image and instruction once, then conditions each action prediction on the latent state and updates it with an action-conditioned GRU. Using Qwen2.5-VL as the backbone, SSVR achieves 99.5/99.6, 96.3/98.0, and 83.9/90.6 EM/PR on FrozenLake, Maze, and MiniBehavior, substantially outperforming prior methods. Extensive experiments support the effectiveness of recurrent state modeling for VLA open-loop planning across input transformations and transfer settings. By reusing static visual-textual context and updating a compact recurrent state, SSVR supports efficient multi-step inference, achieving up to $98.58\times$ faster Maze decoding rollouts than the evaluated baselines with the prefix cache prebuilt.

items.title: Using the Whole Slice: AlphaFold2 Inference on an Eight-Chip TPU v5e
items.summary: arXiv:2609.34818v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AlphaFold2 is written in JAX. JAX treats each chip of a tensor processing unit (TPU) slice as a separate device. A JAX program does not spread its work over the chips by itself, so a user who runs AlphaFold2 on a slice can pay for chips that do nothing. We found no published measurement of how AlphaFold2 inference uses a multi-chip TPU slice. Our goal was to measure how much of an eight-chip TPU v5e slice AlphaFold2 inference uses, and which way of mapping the work in JAX uses all of it. Across 12 experiments, the model used random weights, so we studied execution, not prediction quality. By default, only one chip held data. Batching up to eight input sequences (queries) of 118 residues on one chip with JAX's vmap did not raise throughput. Mapping independent queries to the chips with JAX's pmap ran them in parallel on all eight chips. On a grid of 1 to 8 chips and 100 to 1000 residues, eight chips gave 6.5 to 7.9 times the throughput of one chip. JAX's automatic partitioning did not shorten the call for one query. Our program did not tell the partitioner how to split any array across the chips.

items.title: MiDShip: Multimodal Dataset of Ship Cargo Hold Structures for Engineering Design
items.summary: arXiv:2610.02214v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ship structures govern a vessel's strength, safety, and manufacturability. Their design is governed by classification-society rules comprising hundreds of requirements, making the design process complex and highly iterative. However, data-driven structural design is limited by the lack of large, structured datasets that connect design geometry with structural geometric measures and rule-based constraints. This paper presents MiDShip, a multimodal dataset of 12,753 synthetically generated cargo-hold structural designs for machine learning and optimization. It contains 6,020 randomly generated designs, 496 designs produced by a stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD)-inspired procedure, and 6,237 designs produced by an equation-informed repair procedure. Each retained design includes a parametric vector, full 3D geometries and simplified geometries formatted for finite-element analysis (FEA) meshing, engineering drawings and corresponding annotated versions, a bill of materials, and structural geometric measures. The dataset also includes twenty-five constraints formulated from classification society rules for stiffener spacing, thickness, and section modulus requirements. Full-vessel loading, buckling, fatigue, and ice-class checks are outside the present scope. The primary contribution is the dataset and codebase, two design-generation studies demonstrate their use rather than introduce new optimization algorithms. MiDShip supports future research in machine learning, generative design, and automated rule-based evaluation for ship structures.

items.title: Motion Without State: Probing Dynamical Consistency and Conditioning Bias in Video Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.05135v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Image-to-video models serve as visual world priors whose plausible motion departs from physical simulation. We ask what dynamical structure replaces forward state propagation in generated motion, and how it biases quantitative physics evaluation. Holding law and initial state fixed, we vary visible geometry, prompt wording, and clip length across nine models and compare tracked trajectories against simulator rollouts. Generated motion splits into local visual cues and global boundary control, omitting the propagating physical state between them. Locally, tempo-normalized speed follows track undulations with a 15{\deg}-41{\deg} phase lead toward steepest descent as mean slope barely accelerates the ball, showing short memory of past slope. Local responses fail to compose: no single contact law describes a model's bounces (prescribed, self-calibrated on single-deflector contacts, or fitted in-sample), and balls clear 43 of 49 barriers above release height under an outcome-free prompt. Globally, naming the catch tray lifts arrival 14-76 percentage points above post-contact simulator rollouts, and event duration scales near-linearly with clip length, making apparent gravity 5.6-7.3 times higher in 3 s than in 8 s clips. These patterns persist on photographed first frames, motivating neutral-prompt controls, exit-state rollouts, and tempo-normalized metrics.

items.title: Learning joint predictive distributions from observations with coordinate-aware covariance bounds
items.summary: arXiv:2610.09898v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantifying uncertainty in derived quantities requires forecasts that capture cross-variable dependence. From station observations alone, CLARA predicts the mean and full covariance of a Gaussian joint distribution in one forward pass per lead, trains on a CPU and recalibrates the covariance without altering correlations. On two nationwide Korean weather networks, ten regions on six continents and a nationwide air-quality network, CLARA outperforms learned comparators in lead-mean energy score, by 5.2-5.5% against comparably sized iTransformers with the same temporal-phase inputs on the Korean networks, with gains that persist in two held-out seasons. We prove that the same lower bound on the Cholesky diagonal admits different covariances in different output coordinates. Changing only these coordinates lowers the pressure-difference continuous ranked probability score by 40-67%, lets the learned correlations outperform a fixed correlation matrix in joint likelihood at every lead and, on an electricity grid, improves the joint likelihood with two other backbones.

items.title: Urbex: Agentic Spatial Grounding for City-Scale 3D Scenes
items.summary: arXiv:2610.18356v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: City-scale 3D grounding is commonly formulated as candidate ranking, which requires precomputed instance proposals and becomes inefficient in large outdoor scenes. We propose Urbex, an agentic vision-language framework that instead casts grounding as active spatial search. Urbex represents a city-scale 3D scene as an interactive multi-view environment, allowing a VLM agent to query landmarks, zoom into local regions, render oblique views, and commit a grounded bounding box. We optimize this tool-use policy with reinforcement learning on CityRefer, using smooth localization rewards and lightweight shaping rewards for efficient exploration. Experiments show that Urbex achieves the best Hit@1 and IoU on CityRefer, supports candidate-free grounding without ground-truth boxes, and is substantially faster than the strongest city-scale ranking baseline. Zero-shot results on STPLS3D-Refer further indicate improved cross-scene robustness.

items.title: Find the Fungible: Variable-Resolution Tokenization that Compacts Semantics with a Granularity Dial as a VLM "Catalyst"
items.summary: arXiv:2610.18690v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Efficient vision-language models should preserve a useful representation of the whole image, even under tight budgets. However, aggressive pruning or indiscriminate merging can erase critical details and disrupt the spatial structure. We thus propose Varest, which maximizes semantic fungibility: tokens describing coherent content can be summarized together with minimal information loss. Object boundaries distilled from a visual foundation model guide grouping, while text localization protects details needed for reading. At lower budgets, Varest merges the image into coarser semantic regions, while maintaining full spatial coverage. items.title: FlashReFocus: Interactive Image Refocusing in Seconds
items.summary: arXiv:2610.23297v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Single-image refocusing changes the focal plane and depth of field of a photograph after capture. Users compare focal choices on one photograph, so content stability across edits matters alongside quality and speed. Recent generative methods rerun large diffusion models for every edit, even when they first restore an all-in-focus image, so content can change inconsistently between edits. Yet only this restoration is highly ill-posed and benefits from a generative prior, whereas rendering blur is largely determined by depth and the focal plane. We therefore propose FlashReFocus, which runs diffusion once per photograph and renders each edit with a lightweight network. A one-step diffusion deblurrer with a decoder refiner recovers fine detail efficiently while balancing fidelity and perceptual quality. The renderer uses an explicit defocus map for control and defocus-bias attention to promote information exchange between tokens with similar blur magnitudes. Because every edit reuses the same reconstruction, in-focus content stays consistent across edits, and editing the map enables tilt-shift and two-plane effects. We further collect 3CReal, a benchmark of 89 pairs from three camera-lens systems, to evaluate generalization to unseen optics. For zero-shot bokeh rendering on EBB! Val176 and 3CReal, FlashReFocus leads the evaluated methods in fidelity and perceptual quality. At 1536x1536, a complete refocus takes 2.45 s and each subsequent edit 0.46 s on one RTX PRO 6000.

items.title: Red-Teaming Multi-Agent Attacks for Loss-of-Control Risks
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24052v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI agents are growing more capable and persistent, and are being deployed in ever larger numbers. As more start collaborating, AI control measures must remain effective when they covertly collude on a harmful objective. We introduce MiniLab, a synthetic series of live services and codebases (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives), adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure. We demonstrate distributed attacks, in which different agents carry out separate attack fragments, and how their covertness evades frontier monitors when reading their trajectories individually. We show how distributed attacks spread across diverse contexts and harmful objectives through 16 human-optimized attacks (weight exfiltration, unmonitored rogue deployment, permission elevation, and more). A frontier monitor, GPT-5.6 Sol, reading each agent separately flags only 3.4% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 82.4% when a single agent carries out the same side task. Individual attacks can also be composed into longer attack sequences toward a greater loss-of-control outcome, without any individual agent being flagged. Finally, we tested whether models can plan these covert attacks: even with execution and monitor feedback, the best model-planned attacks succeed covertly under both their feedback monitor and GPT-5.6 Sol in at most 32% of executions, compared with 82% for human-crafted plans, though this may scale with model capabilities. By turning worst-case coordinated attacks into reproducible red-team cases, our work provides a foundation for preventing locally benign agent actions from accumulating into system-level loss of control.

items.title: The Missing Compliance Class: LLM Graders That Collapse Jailbreak Success, and a Free Check
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24872v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Jailbreak evaluations often substitute open-weight 7B to 9B instruction-tuned models as local, deterministic judges for frontier APIs. Holding target models, prompts, responses, and a four-class rubric fixed across eight graders from five organizations, we find that dense 8B and 9B judges collapse compliant responses onto evasion. One assigns compliance zero times in 900 responses while agreeing with our reference judge on 78.0% of items, certifying an unsafe model as safe. This collapse holds across four 900-response corpora, multiplying reported compliance by a factor of 22 to 25 on our primary corpora while non-refusal shifts by 18.0 to 23.0 points. Without the three collapsing graders, compliance varies by 1.7x to 2.8x across all four corpora, whereas post-labelling rubric rulings (+16.3 points) and benchmark choice (15.3 points) still shift non-refusal. Per-class label counts expose class collapse at zero cost without human labels, motivating an eight-item reporting minimum that pairs compliance with non-refusal rates.

items.title: One Evaluation Is Enough: Inversion-Free Image Editing with Trajectory Correction
items.summary: arXiv:2610.30827v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Real-image editing commonly relies on inversion and iterative sampling, while efficient one-step editors often stabilize a large update by estimating and averaging editing fields at multiple noise levels. We ask a stricter question: is a single temporal field evaluation sufficient for reliable inversion-free editing? Our answer rests on a previously underused duality in a variance-preserving (VP) one-step model: one source-target query at a shared noisy state simultaneously determines a local angular semantic tangent and a clean endpoint displacement. We integrate the tangent over the analytically known remaining VP angle to obtain a nominal one-step transport, and use the endpoint displacement to correct its long-horizon extrapolation through a constrained projection. This transport-first, correction-second construction yields Endpoint-Calibrated Transport (ECT), a closed-form, training-free editor requiring only one noise level, two text conditions packed into one denoiser batch, and one latent update. ECT requires no image inversion, trajectory integration, second temporal observation, or iterative optimization, and can be directly applied to pretrained epsilon-prediction VP one-step generators. Across the reported benchmark settings, ECT delivers stable gains in editing quality within an extremely short editing time.

items.title: EvolveMAS: A Unified Self-Evolution Framework for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34450v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Decentralized multi-agent systems (MAS) enable large language model agents to interact without centralized control. Agents need to adapt to other agents at test time and reuse accumulated experience to refine their interaction strategies for future interactions across cooperative, mixed-motive, and adversarial settings. However, existing approaches often develop adaptation mechanisms for particular interaction settings. This raises a central question: how can decentralized MAS support test-time adaptation and reliable experience reuse across interaction settings? We propose EvolveMAS, a unified self-evolution framework that supports experience-driven adaptation within and across episodes. EvolveMAS pairs each main agent with a dedicated MemoryAgent for test-time memory governance, which maintains isolated Structured Memory outside the main agent's reasoning context. EvolveMAS organizes adaptation into two complementary processes: Within-Episode Online Adaptation and Cross-Episode Knowledge Evolution. During Within-Episode Online Adaptation, MemoryAgent updates episodic, semantic, and working memory from interaction evidence to inform subsequent actions. During Cross-Episode Knowledge Evolution, the main agent uses memory and episode outcomes to distill reusable interaction knowledge comprising partner profiles and interaction strategies for subsequent episodes. Across five benchmarks and six evaluation configurations spanning the three interaction settings, EvolveMAS achieves the highest normalized average score of 77.2 among the compared methods. Ablations show that test-time memory governance and cross-episode knowledge reuse both improve performance. Interaction traces further illustrate how updated memory and distilled knowledge guide subsequent interactions. These results support experience-driven adaptation in decentralized MAS without updating model parameters.

items.title: Ranking Function Generation with LLMs for Termination
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35523v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ranking functions are a fundamental technique for proving loop termination, but synthesizing them remains challenging and often requires substantial expertise. Despite considerable progress in their automated synthesis, existing approaches remain limited in their effectiveness. We propose RAINFALL, a neuro-symbolic framework that tightly integrates large language models (LLMs) with symbolic verification. To our best knowledge, RAINFALL is the first to employ a generate-verify-refine paradigm for LLM-based ranking function synthesis. RAINFALL formulates ranking function synthesis as a constrained code-completion task, inserting placeholders into the input program that the LLM must fill in four predefined slots per loop. The resulting program is checked by a symbolic verifier. Successful verification yields a valid ranking function, while verification failures produce diagnostics that are translated into natural-language feedback to guide iterative refinement. We evaluate RAINFALL on two public benchmark suites comprising 358 terminating C programs. Using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, RAINFALL synthesizes verified ranking functions for 333 programs (93.02%), outperforming all evaluated baselines. Notably, it solves 22 more programs than PROTON 2.1, the winner of the SV-COMP 2026 Termination Category. Combining RAINFALL with PROTON 2.1 further increases the success rate to 96.65% (346/358 programs). Ablation studies demonstrate the contributions of placeholder contracts, few-shot examples, symbolic verification, and diagnostic feedback, while experiments across different LLMs establish the broader applicability of the framework.
