items.title: Atom as an Agent: Emergent Order by Collective Predictive Coding
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36673v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: What is the intrinsic reason of emergence of macroscopic order parameter out of microscopic systems? In this article, we apply to physics the collective predictive coding (CPC), the theory of language/symbol emergence. As our language emerges out of our human communications, physical macroscopic order parameter emerges out of communications among atoms --- each atom is regarded as an agent who predicts each other's behavior through inference. We present three examples of classical spin systems: two-dimensional ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, a two-dimensional spin model with competing stripe orders, and the fully connected Sherrington--Kirkpatrick spin-glass model. In all of these examples, proper macroscopic order parameters including the replica overlap emerge automatically through communication informatics of CPC, only from observed spin configurations. We call the learned macroscopic coordinate the collective predictive order. Furthermore, for the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, the equilibrium distribution of the collective predictive order yields an emergent potential with the symmetry and thermal evolution characteristic of a Landau potential. Notably, the emergence of the collective predictive order does not refer to any structure of microscopic Hamiltonians/Lagrangians. Thus our ``Atom-as-an-Agent" (AaaA) principle offers a completely data-driven method for the emergence of macroscopic order, that is, machine learning physics.

items.title: Confidence-Aware Speed-over-Ground Estimation from Doppler Spectra via Reconstruction-Based Representation Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40253v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reliable speed-over-ground estimation from ground-facing Doppler spectra is essential for mobile platforms such as railway systems. Classical signal-processing approaches can provide accurate estimates under favorable conditions, but often degrade in challenging conditions. We propose confidence-aware speed-over-ground estimation trained on rail-domain data that estimates speed over ground and frame-level confidence from Doppler spectra with several novel contributions: First, we transfer the idea of exploiting a reconstruction task by an autoencoder for performance estimation from previous work to Doppler RaDAR. Second, we append a speed-over-ground estimation head operating on the autoencoder's latent space features. Third, we omit the reconstruction decoder during inference but add a low-cost dedicated confidence head for frame-wise error-bound estimation. Fourth, we reveal how noise augmentation training can provide high robustness to the method. Experiments show that our approach improves speed estimation accuracy over classical baselines while providing informative confidence estimates that indicate the reliability of individual predictions, even under adverse signal conditions.

items.title: Intervenable Concept Dynamics for Video Activity Forecasting
items.summary: arXiv:2611.00020v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Concept bottleneck models route predictions through human-understandable concepts, making their intermediate states inspectable and editable. Extending this model family to forecasting requires modeling how concept activations evolve over time as objects, actions, and their interactions change, yet existing CBMs ground concepts only in observed inputs and do not forecast their future evolution. We study this problem using videos of ongoing activities and forecast future activities through a named-concept state. We propose TRACE-CBM (Temporal Relational Activity Concept Evolution), which first refines observed concept activations with sparse spatio-temporal graphs. It then recursively predicts future concept states, conditioning each transition on the prior activity distribution, and decodes both observed and predicted states with a shared activity classifier. At inference time, the model supports editing concept values, activity activations, and learned edges without parameter updates, exposing the relational spatio-temporal dependencies used for forecasting. Across multiple datasets, TRACE improves observed-activity accuracy over concept-based methods and stays close to matched black-box forecasters in forecast accuracy. Intervention experiments show that concept edits correct part of the initially incorrect forecasts without flipping initially correct ones, and that activity-belief edits can steer forecasts toward a requested activity. Code: https://github.com/patrick-knab/TRACE-CBM

items.title: Demystifying Prompt Stealing Attacks against Synthetic Video
items.summary: arXiv:2611.00102v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Creators publicly showcase generated content to advertise and sell their work, but these examples may also enable unauthorized reproduction and customization. We study whether an adversary can derive reusable inputs from a single public video for faithful reconstruction and controlled editing, without access to the original prompt or generator. We adapt captioning and prompt optimization approaches to video prompt stealing attacks (PSAs) and find that prompt recovery alone provides limited reconstruction fidelity. Even the original prompt produces different spatial and temporal realizations when the initial noise changes. Using an independent generator enlarges the reconstruction gap, as reusing the original prompt and seed can still produce substantially different videos. We propose V-PSA, which uses a recovered caption and DDIM inversion to construct a reference trajectory under an independent generator. Null-Text Inversion then optimizes per-step unconditional embeddings to reduce deviations from this trajectory during reconstruction. The resulting inputs also guide generation when the caption is modified, supporting edits that change selected content while preserving the target's layout and motion. We construct a benchmark containing 12,000 video-prompt pairs from three victim generators and four prompt sources. V-PSA achieves video-to-video similarity around 0.9 between target and reconstructed videos, substantially improving over prompt-only baselines with similarity score of 0.6, and supports multiple controlled variations that preserve the target's structure. Additional experiments show that augmenting prior image PSAs with inversion-derived inputs also improves reconstruction. Our results show that evaluations restricted to prompt recovery can underestimate an attacker's ability to reconstruct public generative outputs.

items.title: dKV Forcing: Separating Generation and Memory Representations through a Differentiable KV Cache
items.summary: arXiv:2611.01648v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A causal video generator writes every segment it produces into a key--value (KV) cache, and later segments know the past only through it. Self-rollout training stops the gradient at this cache, and Self Gradient Forcing (SGF) restores it, but applies it to the same weights that generate the current segment. We find that writing and generating are different roles: in a pretrained generator the written KV already differs from the KV used for denoising, and on shared weights the gradient from future reads is negatively aligned with the gradient of generation. We propose dKV Forcing (dKV denotes differentiable KV), which gives the write its own parameters, a low-rank residual used only when a segment enters the cache, and trains them with the gradient of the later segments that read what they wrote. Opening this gradient through the cache in common use exhausts GPU memory. We trace this to checkpoint replay re-writing the cache, not to the gradient path, which removes the need for the second reconstruction pass of SGF. dKV Forcing keeps the cache as persistent differentiable pages and computes the exact gradient in one temporal traversal, with an $11\%$ lower memory peak and $28\%$ less resident memory. With pages that store hidden states, it trains 15\,s clips on which the two-pass reconstruction runs out of memory. Trained on 5\,s clips, dKV Forcing reaches the highest VBench-Long quality score at 60\,s and 240\,s and outperforms SGF by $3.6$ and $6.1$ points of aesthetic quality, with a higher dynamic degree.

items.title: How many sorted projections determine any n points in k dimensions?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06470v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Let $d_1,\dots,d_m$ be directions in $\mathbb{R}^k$, where $k\ge 2$. A multiset $X$ of $n$ points of $\mathbb{R}^k$ projects to the $m$ multisets of numbers $\{\{x\cdot d_j : x\in X\}\}$, or equivalently to the $m$ sorted lists of these numbers. How many directions are needed for these projections to determine every multiset of $n$ points? Two simple bounds are known in every dimension: more than $(k-1)\log_2 n$ directions are always needed, and $(k-1)n+1$ directions in general position always suffice. In the plane much more is known: Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron showed that almost every choice of $O(\log n \log\log n)$ directions suffices. Whether anything similar holds in higher dimensions was left open by Dym, Wellershoff, Tsoukanis, Levy and Balan. We observe that two lemmas of Hair and Sahai, proved for list recovery of random linear codes, answer that question, and by tightening their argument we show that in every dimension almost every choice of $(4k-2)\ln(2n)\ln(k\log_2 2n)+k+1$ directions suffices. For $k\le 10$ this beats the linear bound once $n$ is larger than about 100: for example, 144 directions suffice for multisets of 1000 points in the plane, and an exact computation lowers this to 133. Letting some of the random blocks in their argument fail removes a factor $\log k$: almost every choice of $O(k\log n\log\log n)$ directions suffices, uniformly in $k$ and $n$. We also show that $2k-1$ directions never determine three points, so that the logarithmic lower bound is not tight; that every $m$ directions in the plane fail on some pair of multisets of size $O(1.65^m)$, improving the bound $O(1.80^m)$ of Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron; and that for each $k$, $m$ and $n$, either almost every choice of $m$ directions works or almost none does.

items.title: Greedy BPE with Replacement Counts Achieves the Tight Approximation Ratio $(1-e^{-2})/2$
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08671v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) builds the tokenisers of many language models by repeatedly merging a most frequent adjacent pair of symbols. Kozma and Voderholzer showed that $k$ greedy merges save, in the worst case, between $1/3$ and $(1-e^{-2})/2 \approx 0.43233$ of what the best $k$ merges save, and asked for the exact constant. We resolve this question for the replacement-count rule they analyse. For every string and weighted word table, every budget $k$, and every tie-breaking rule, greedy saves at least $\frac12(1-(1-2/k)^k)$ of the optimum. This establishes the exact worst-case approximation ratio $(1-e^{-2})/2$, approached as $k\to\infty$ but never attained. The proof is based on a shadow inequality: after $i$ greedy steps, the optimum is at most $2G_i+kg_{i+1}$, where $G_i$ is greedy's saving so far and $g_{i+1}$ its next gain. We also show that the worst-case ratio at budget $k$ exceeds the limiting constant by $\Theta(k^{-1/2})$. For the overlapping-count rule used by deployed trainers, we prove a lower bound greater than $0.38954$ and an asymptotic upper bound of approximately $0.40407$; determining its exact constant remains open.

items.title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09892v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2% and 42.9% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation. See https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-amp/ for code and videos.

items.title: RoadState: A Domain-Prior-Enhanced Vision-Language System for Industrial-Grade Lane-Level Map Updating
items.summary: arXiv:2611.10746v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Lane-level maps provide foundational structured road information for navigation, intelligent driving, and intelligent transportation systems. Understanding road-scene semantics from structural and contextual cues is essential for reliable lane-level map updating, yet remains challenging in production due to occlusions, ambiguous lane markings, temporary obstacles, and viewpoint changes, while downstream workflows require temporally consistent, physically valid, and auditable outputs rather than free-form descriptions. We present RoadState, a production-deployed vision-language system that transforms sequential road-scene observations into structured lane-level semantics for Baidu Maps' map-updating pipeline. Its core model, RoadState-VLM, formulates road-scene understanding as autoregressive state estimation, predicting the current structured road state from the previous observation, previous symbolic state, and current observation. To improve semantic consistency and reasoning fidelity across interdependent road-state dimensions, we introduce Geometric Chain-of-Thought (Geo-CoT), which encodes a directed acyclic graph of semantic dependencies as a domain prior. On a real-world dataset, RoadState-VLM achieves 94.33% mean accuracy across six road-state dimensions, outperforming the strongest fine-tuned VLM baseline, with ablations confirming the complementary gains of Geo-CoT and temporal transition context. In production, a cascaded routing pipeline directs routine cases to lightweight models and reserves complex cases for RoadState-VLM. Deployed since March 2025, RoadState supports lane-level map updating across 360+ cities, reduces overall production costs by 30%, and maintains robust performance under stress testing with human-in-the-loop auditing.

items.title: Off-Policy RL with Online Inference Tuning: 1st Place Solution to the CoRL 2026 RoboEval Challenge
items.summary: arXiv:2611.11464v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The CoRL 2026 RoboEval challenge has eight bimanual tasks, and it ranks a policy not only on whether it succeeds but on how: every stage of the task, done safely, efficiently and with both arms in coordination, scored against human demonstrations. My solution has two parts. The generic part, carried over from my LeHome challenge solution, is off-policy RL on a $\pi_{0.5}$-based policy that is also its own value function. It is trained with AWR and RECAP on advantages of the exact official score, in a loop where every rollout is at the same time a Thompson-sampling trial of about 20 inference parameters. Out of the box, it took the policy to 0.85 RDS on held-out seeds in two days (and it was still very far from convergence). The competition-specific part adds data that local exploration cannot find: generated demonstrations that reach the full reward, and recovery episodes that start from the policy's own failures. The submitted policy reaches 0.990 RDS on my held-out seeds and 0.987 on the official seeds, and it won first place in the challenge, with 0.988 in the organisers' final evaluation on 1,000 unpublished seeds per task.

items.title: From Attack Surface to Defense Architecture: Compositional Security for Agentic Coding Harnesses
items.summary: arXiv:2611.13960v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI coding harnesses couple language models to shells, filesystems, and network sockets so that agents can resolve issues and run tests. That coupling turns the harness into an automated Living-off-the-Land (LotL) platform: once an adversary can inject instructions into retrieved content, dual-use binaries such as bash, curl, and find become the payload rather than a vulnerability to be separately exploited. We argue that security in agentic systems is not an emergent behavioral property of individual language models, but a structural property of the cognitive architecture and of the composition of permissions across interacting agents and humans. Static regex blacklists miss flag permutations and structural attacks, whereas LLM-as-a-Judge guardrails ask a second model to guess physical invariants at tens to hundreds of milliseconds per call while over-blocking benign work. We present ActiveSecHarness, a neurosymbolic reference-monitor architecture organized around Separation of Intelligence and Authority across four pillars: (1) Macaroon-inspired HMAC capability tokens across four Trust and Authority Rings; (2) a product taint lattice L_trust x L_sens and a compositional Separation-of-Duties ledger over shared workspace provenance; (3) deterministic OS/subprocess guards; and (4) extended bytecode certificates, split-horizon dual-key audit logs, a self-healing verification loop (CodeVerifier, DualModelReviewer, SecurityTestSynthesizer), and a progressive pedagogical UserWikiManager. On N=252 fixtures and a 12+12 multi-step trajectory suite, Ring 0 achieves FPR=0.000 (0.939 unfitted out-of-sample / 0.962 OS-inert; 1.000 post-audit conformance ABR) in 31.5 us median latency (4,517x faster than a live local LLM-judge) and blocks 12/12 multi-step kill chains at 0.000 benign trajectory FPR (266.7 us/step; ~24 us/step O(1) ledger state folding).

items.title: Editable Video Context: Mid-Context KV-Cache Reuse for Context-Managing Video LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18718v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Context Language Models let a model edit its own context, while Suffix Cache Reuse makes edits to text efficient by adjusting the positions of cached keys for surviving tokens. We extend these ideas to video language models with multimodal rotary position embeddings (M-RoPE). We represent a long video as timestamped segments. After viewing a sparsely sampled version, the model selects segments for decoding at 4x the frame rate, and the remaining segments are removed from its context. Our rebuild method reuses the KV cache of surviving segments by rotating their keys with a single offset shared by the temporal, height, and width components of Qwen2.5-VL's M-RoPE. A content-hashed cache also avoids repeating vision-encoder computation for those segments. In preliminary experiments with Qwen2.5-VL-7B on synthetic needle-in-a-video-haystack questions over public-domain films, the method reduces prefill tokens and end-to-end rebuild latency relative to full recomputation while usually producing the same answer. Densifying the segment containing the answer improves accuracy when that segment is known. When the model selects segments itself, accuracy does not improve: it rarely identifies a needle that was absent from the sparse sample. We release the code, raw logs, and scripts used to reproduce the paper's results.

items.title: As Student Rollouts Continue, Visual Backdoors Keep Growing
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22446v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conventional knowledge distillation can facilitate the propagation of backdoors from teacher models to student models. However, how this risk manifests in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remains insufficiently studied. OPD has recently emerged as an important post-training paradigm for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Unlike traditional offline distillation, OPD does not require teacher-generated responses. Instead, it uses the teacher's probability distributions to supervise response trajectories generated online by the student. Since the initial student model typically generates benign responses and receives no explicit supervision from malicious target responses, OPD appears to offer some inherent resistance to backdoor propagation. In this paper, we challenge this intuition and reveal a more subtle risk of visual backdoor propagation in OPD. Through experiments across multiple model families and datasets, together with theoretical analysis, we identify three main findings. First, unlike the relatively gradual propagation observed in traditional offline distillation, backdoors rarely emerge in OPD at low poisoning ratios. However, the attack success rate rapidly approaches 100% once a critical threshold is exceeded. Second, backdoor propagation does not depend on explicit malicious responses. Instead, it is driven by the continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass assigned by the teacher. Finally, based on these findings, we propose a novel trigger design that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection. These findings further reveal an overlooked mechanism of backdoor propagation in OPD and highlight its potential security risks.

items.title: LoopZip: Visual Token Compression for Efficient Looped Vision-Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22728v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Looped vision-language models (VLMs) deepen computation by reusing shared layers, approaching larger models' capabilities with fewer parameters and easing the storage and deployment burden of stacking independent layers. However, repeatedly processing long visual sequences still incurs substantial compute and GPU memory costs. Visual token compression reduces these costs by shortening sequences. Existing methods mainly select original tokens directly or combine selection with aggregation. In looped models, the former may overlook changing token importance across calls and discard information needed later; the latter lack joint consideration of output changes across calls, limiting information preservation. We propose LoopZip, a training-free visual token compression algorithm addressing both issues. Visual aggregation builds a compact candidate pool before the looped backbone, and cross-invocation selection averages instruction attention from the first two existing calls of the same shared attention layer to retain tokens needed by both states. Weight-tied value correction then jointly fits shared visual-value adjustments to both pre-selection layer outputs, reducing output deviations across states. To validate LoopZip's effectiveness, we conduct extensive experiments covering two open-source looped VLMs, eleven benchmarks, and three pruning ratios. On LoopVL-1B, LoopZip retains 97.16% of the original model's performance at 50% pruning ratio and exceeds the strongest baseline by 5.36% at 87.5% pruning ratio. Across Hugging Face Transformers, vLLM, and SGLang, LoopVL-1B with LoopZip reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 58.36%-58.98% and achieves 2.01-2.47x end-to-end speedups over the original model.

items.title: Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23211v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. We plan to publicly release the code and data.

items.title: Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge
items.summary: arXiv:2611.24637v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.

items.title: MADJEPA: Enhanced Multi-Stage Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Medical Anomaly Detection
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25194v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Anomaly detection in medical images is a complex task, requiring the development of a robust model using only healthy patient data. Without access to labeled data, modern approaches typically employ self-supervised learning to obtain a model of normality. Since world models promise to build strong internal representations of their environment, we consider them as suitable candidates for the medical anomaly detection environment, namely medical investigations of healthy patients. To this end, we propose MADJEPA, a medical anomaly detector based on an enhanced multi-stage joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). We design a multi-stage training pipeline to produce a robust detector: (1) image-based JEPA (I-JEPA) training aims to learn a strong representation of normal training data; (2) target encoder distillation aims to modulate over-generalization of I-JEPA representations to abnormal data; (3) pseudo-anomaly classification aims to calibrate anomaly predictions by learning a tight boundary around the normal data manifold. To demonstrate our design, we carry out comprehensive experiments on six datasets covering various medical image domains (e.g. MRI, OCT, X-ray, histopathology), comparing our MADJEPA with numerous state-of-the-art methods. The results show that our carefully designed world model, MADJEPA, attains competitive results, ranking first on three datasets. Our ablation studies further confirm the utility of each training stage, indicating that I-JEPA alone is not sufficient to obtain competitive results in medical anomaly detection. We publicly release our code at https://github.com/Sabina085/madjepa.

items.title: Loop-OPF: Solver-Informed Learning for Optimal Power Flow with Inference-Time Topology Adaptivity
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27013v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learning for optimal power flow (OPF) has recently been advocated to accelerate OPF solutions by using a pre-trained neural network (NN) to predict directly from given inputs such as the load demand. However, existing learning-for-OPF methods largely fall short of ensuring the optimality and feasibility of their predictions. They also struggle to adapt at inference time to unseen topology scenarios, such as those caused by line or generator outages. This work puts forth Loop-OPF, a solver-informed NN that builds its layers from the iterations of the primal-dual hybrid gradient (PDHG) method. Under standard convexity and regularity conditions on DC-OPF, the resultant fixed-point output of Loop-OPF is thus optimal and feasible. To speed up PDHG across diverse OPF scenarios, Loop-OPF learns certain PDHG parameters in a self-supervised manner, without any OPF solution labels. We adopt the deep equilibrium (DEQ) framework for training so that the memory cost does not grow with the number of layers. As the grid topology enters every layer as an input, the same trained Loop-OPF directly adapts to unseen contingencies without retraining. Numerical tests on the IEEE 300-bus and PEGASE 1354-, 2869-, and 9241-bus networks have demonstrated the accuracy and topology adaptivity of the proposed Loop-OPF over competing learning-for-OPF methods.

items.title: VMSA: Video Memory Skill Agent for Long Video Understanding
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27381v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Long-video question answering requires retrieving and integrating relevant evidence from videos spanning hours or even days. Recent agentic approaches organize video information into external memories and iteratively retrieve evidence to answer questions. However, effective retrieval and reasoning remain challenging, as agents must determine what information to search for, which memory sources to access, and how to connect evidence across distant temporal intervals. To address these challenges, we propose Video Memory Skill Agent (VMSA), a framework that jointly designs structured video memories and memory skills for long-video understanding. VMSA constructs three complementary memory components. Segment Caption Memory and Entity Event Memory serve as searchable evidence sources, while Entity-Aware Episode Memory provides broad yet detailed video context to guide evidence retrieval and reasoning. To further support effective memory utilization, VMSA induces memory skills from successful agent trajectories, incrementally refining or extending a compact skill library to guide iterative evidence retrieval, reasoning, and verification. Across seven long-video question-answering benchmarks, VMSA achieves the highest accuracy on all three week-long egocentric benchmarks, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.4% on Ego-R1 Bench, and the best or competitive performance on four additional benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of all three memory components and memory skills, with memory skills also improving temporal evidence localization.

items.title: Self-Supervised Continuous-Time Depth Learning and Ego-Motion Estimation from Asynchronous Events
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27509v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Event cameras register brightness changes pixel by pixel with microsecond precision, whereas the dense depth that could supervise them is costly to acquire and exists only at isolated instants. Condensing the stream into frames eases learning, but at the expense of the very timing that sets event sensing apart. We propose a self-supervised approach in which each event is assigned its own depth in continuous time, and the camera motion is recovered from the same observations. Supervision arises from geometry: lifted into 3D by its predicted depth and displaced by the camera motion at the instant it fired, an event should coincide with others produced by the same edge, so any misalignment exposes an error in depth or motion. Differentiable rendering then turns these per-event estimates into dense depth maps at target times within each window, faithful to the events behind them. On MVSEC, the approach outperforms prior event-only self-supervised methods in most sequences and depth ranges, with the widest margins at night, and recovers camera rotation more accurately than an earlier unsupervised event-based method. Ablations isolate the roles of local spatiotemporal context, the temporal backbone, and the alignment objective. These results position motion-compensated event alignment as a principled source of supervision for continuous-time depth and ego-motion estimation.

items.title: Social sycophancy differs across access modes of large language models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28012v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can display sycophancy, a tendency to excessively praise, agree with, or validate a user. Existing studies have tested LLMs for sycophancy primarily through application programming interfaces (APIs) rather than the consumer user interfaces (UIs) through which the public commonly interacts with LLMs. Access mode (API vs. UI) may affect observed sycophancy rates. However, it remains unknown to what extent prominent models show API-UI differences in social sycophancy, which includes behaviors potentially more likely in UIs (e.g., softening warranted criticism). We tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek through both APIs and UIs on four dimensions of social sycophancy. Across models, UI access was generally associated with greater social sycophancy, with odds ratios up to 7.56 (95% CI [6.22, 9.20]). However, UI-API differences varied significantly across models for all sycophancy dimensions, including a pronounced reversal for DeepSeek moral sycophancy (43% UI vs. 82.3% API). Overall, our results suggest that API-based LLM evaluations may underestimate the prevalence of sycophancy in corresponding consumer-facing systems, making access conditions consequential for the external validity of LLM evaluation. To facilitate research on access-mode effects, we release 57,000 model responses and SycoUI, a browser-automation pipeline for standardized cross-interface LLM evaluation.

items.title: Learning in the Passive Space: End-to-End Muti-Order Port-Hamiltonian Macromodeling
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28778v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Compact, passive state-space macromodels of interconnects and power-delivery networks are essential for stable transient signal- and power-integrity simulations. However, conventional flows require costly per-layout full-wave electromagnetic (EM) simulations, while both traditional fitting and prior learning surrogates rely on post-hoc fitting or passivity perturbation that degrades accuracy without guaranteeing convergence. In this work, we propose an end-to-end macromodeling framework that learns directly in the passive space, mapping physical layout graphs to multi-order port-Hamiltonian (pH) macromodels. Specifically, our network encodes each layout graph into unconstrained matrix blocks and assembles them via a complete, prefix-nested pH parameterization that guarantees continuous-frequency passivity and stability by construction, yielding valid $k$-state macromodels via direct state slicing in one forward pass. To train all orders without reference realizations, we supervise the network directly on S-parameters through a progressive order-growth curriculum. Evaluated on 27k unseen test structures from a 270k-structure advanced-packaging dataset, our framework reduces mean S-parameter error by $42\%$ on average (up to $65\%$) over established macromodeling tools fitted to ground-truth EM responses, achieves zero passivity violations across $459{,}000$ exported models, and accelerates macromodel generation by $11{,}000$--$39{,}000\times$ ($36$--$85$~ms per layout).

items.title: Seeing vs. Knowing: Counterfactual Supervision and Correction for 3D-Aware Object Editing
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29542v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Rotating, translating, or rescaling an object in a photograph requires revealing unseen surfaces, preserving visible appearance, and updating shadows and reflections. Reconstructed 3D assets, rendered at the target pose as a 3D state, provide explicit geometric guidance, but their imperfect textures may conflict with the photograph, while standard paired training does not explicitly teach the editor which source to trust. To address this, we propose counterfactual state supervision, which constructs controlled photo--state conflicts through hidden-surface repainting, hidden geometry with re-rendered shadows and reflections, and visible-surface texture replacement. This teaches the editor to follow the 3D state for unseen content while preserving photograph-visible appearance. However, learning this distinction does not ensure that it is maintained during sampling. We therefore introduce symmetric counterfactual correction, which uses state-side and photo-side twins, which share the photograph and the state respectively, to construct directed latent perturbations toward condition-inconsistent targets and train recovery toward the target specified by the current condition. Both strategies operate only during training, requiring no architectural changes or additional inference steps. Experiments on OBJect and SpatialEdit-Bench demonstrate strong spatial editing performance and content preservation, while controlled ablations show improved source selection and sustained responsiveness to conditioning during sampling.

items.title: Sparse Hodge Preference Optimization: Fine-Tuning Language Models toward Alignment beyond Transitive Preferences
items.summary: arXiv:2611.30135v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The growing adoption of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which leverages pairwise preference data, reflects its great success in fine-tuning large language models to align with human expectations. It directly optimizes the policy from human preferences without explicit reward modeling or the complexities of reinforcement learning-based approaches. However, the classic DPO relies on the Bradley--Terry sampling model and cannot effectively capture intransitivity or cyclic structures in aggregated human preference data. In this article, we propose Sparse Hodge Preference Optimization (SHPO), a preference optimization algorithm that augments DPO with a sparse antisymmetric curl residual motivated by the combinatorial Hodge decomposition. We prove that SHPO strictly enlarges DPO's hypothesis class on comparison graphs containing at least one triangle, under some mild regularity conditions on the response representations. We further establish a theoretical guarantee for $\ell_1$-regularized estimation of the curl coefficients under fixed policy and representations. Qualitative studies on three preference datasets under the same QLoRA budget, SHPO-aligned LLM achieves satisfactory performances in preference accuracy, cyclic structure recovery, and GPT-4o-judged generation quality.

items.title: PixelOne: From Options to Pixels in a Single Forward for GUI Grounding
items.summary: arXiv:2611.30235v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: GUI grounding requires precise clicks at low latency. Recent models such as GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift predict coordinates in one forward pass using fixed global bins with local refinement. However, screenshot downsampling removes detail needed to locate small controls, while fixed bins cover larger pixel ranges at higher resolutions. We introduce PixelOne, which transfers spatial knowledge from a search teacher to a student that predicts clicks directly from screenshots at native resolution. The teacher uses VideoJEV's text-option scorer to select rows and columns and progressively zoom into candidate regions. The student inherits the teacher's parameters and matches its distributions over explored regions through spatial distillation alongside box supervision. At inference, the same decision head selects a visual token, and a lightweight pixel head predicts the click within it, all in one forward pass. A click-aligned loss encourages pixels inside the target box to score above those outside. Across four benchmarks, PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B achieves 83.8% mean accuracy, the highest among the evaluated single-forward grounders, with a mean latency of 0.43 s per target.

items.title: RoboInF: A Benchmark for Instruction Fidelity in Robotic Manipulation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.30555v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Precise language control requires embodied models to follow instructions governing both task outcomes and execution. Although recent methods train policies to follow increasingly detailed commands, existing benchmarks often assess instruction following alongside perception, planning, and generalization to unfamiliar scenes. Higher task success therefore offers limited evidence of closer adherence to instructions. We introduce RoboInF, a benchmark measuring how reliably manipulation policies adapt their behavior to changes in an instruction. For each of eight tasks, six to twelve expert-validated instruction branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation detail while holding the initial scene and robot state fixed. Task-specific checkers verify the terminal goal and use recorded trajectories, contacts, and event sequences to assess compliance throughout execution. The accompanying RoboInF-4K dataset pairs 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived annotations of motion and contact. We evaluate leading manipulation policies ($\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenWAM) and inference-only agents (GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash). All four models exhibit a gap between task completion and faithful execution, indicating substantial room for fine-grained instruction following.

items.title: Lorentz symmetry in self-supervised representation learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.31011v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) and explicit physical inductive biases have driven major advances in jet tagging, yet they are typically pursued along separate tracks. In this work, we unify both paradigms by integrating the Lorentz-equivariant Geometric Algebra Transformer slim (L-GATr-slim) architecture with the LeJEPA framework for representation learning. Pre-training on 100 million jets from the JetClass dataset, we optimize towards a latent space, which is invariant across physics-motivated jet augmentations. We demonstrate that enforcing Lorentz symmetry in the latent space is critical for representation quality and that this can be achieved either architecturally or learned via kinematic augmentations. With a standard non-invariant Transformer backbone, LeJEPA outperforms established autoregressive, masked particle modelling, and self-distillation baselines in linear- and MLP-probe accuracy, with L-GATr-slim providing further complementary gains. Across downstream benchmarks, our pre-trained models consistently outperform baselines trained from scratch or through different pre-training objectives.

With a standard non-invariant Transformer backbone, LeJEPA outperforms established autoregressive, masked particle modelling, and self-distillation baselines in linear- and MLP-probe accuracy, with L-GATr-slim providing further complementary gains. Across downstream benchmarks, our pre-trained models consistently outperform baselines trained from scratch or through different pre-training objectives.

items.title: AI Stocks’ Big Worry: a Chip Glut
items.summary:
If anyone needs therapy nowadays, it may be tech investors more than Jensen Huang. Let’s face it: The stock market has been a little manic-depressive lately. On Tuesday, for instance, the Jensen-reinstatement rally reversed itself, sending Nvidia stock down nearly 6%, while Anthropic closed below its IPO price. Neoclouds such as CoreWeave and Nebius both dropped 11%.

That’s perhaps a sign that there are some things more important to the market than the fate of any one man, even our “geniuses,” as President Trump calls Huang. Among those things are supply and demand for computing capacity, and what that means both for heavily indebted neoclouds and growth expectations for chip suppliers. Worries that we could be headed for a glut of chips have percolated on Wall Street for months, without much evidence of such a surplus. But on Tuesday, SemiAnalysis published a report saying “we are starting to see signs of a broader pricing cooldown” in the market for Nvidia’s AI chips, citing price cuts by SpaceX. Uh oh.

items.title: In Private Funding, Like IPOs, Big Companies Dominate
items.summary:
Shares of Anthropic fell below its $83 IPO price on Tuesday morning, summing up what has been a tough year for IPOs. While a couple of monster IPOs got done—Anthropic and SpaceX—only a handful of others made it through including offerings from SK Hynix, Cerebras and Lime. And as of Tuesday, all of those were trading below their IPO price. 

That makes it the fifth year in a row when the IPO market has been at least a bit disappointing. A bunch of companies are lined up for next year—including OpenAI—but slumping tech valuations fueled by skepticism about the AI boom clouds prospects for 2027. 

In that context, it’s a decent time to take the pulse of startup dealmaking. One thing is clear: as in the IPO market this year, in the private fundraising market, the biggest companies are dominating.

The top 10 private companies have more than doubled their combined valuation from $1.1 trillion to $2.6 trillion in just one year, Goldman’s top tech banker Jane Dunlevie said on stage last week at Goldman Sachs’ annual private tech conference in Las Vegas. 

She was talking about OpenAI, Anthropic, Databricks, Stripe, Waymo, Revolut, Anduril, Ramp, Cognition and Jeff Bezos's Prometheus. And more than half of those—OpenAI, Databricks, Anduril, Stripe, Ramp and Cognition—are now trying to raise billions more.

There’s still plenty of smaller startups emerging. Goldman managed to play matchmaker for more than 400 investors and 400-plus startups in the gilded corridors at the Encore Wynn Hotel. The mood was still electric, though investors are starting to think: as public market valuations fall, how should we value these private companies? 

One reason why private valuations can stay elevated even as public stocks drop is that venture investors tend to zoom in on growth. Many of these AI businesses’ revenues have taken off, even as they bleed money thanks to expensive AI models they run and the chips they need to buy or rent. 

At a fireside chat at last week’s confab, Winston Weinberg, CEO of legal AI startup Harvey, acknowledged that even with fast revenue growth, its gross margins fell to about negative 55% around June. They improved the figure by about 95% in roughly three months. Weinberg said annualized revenue grew from $190 million at the end of last year and expected to end this year with at least $675 million.

“We’re still early in the build out of AI, which means many of the defining companies of this era are not yet public and many investors are just getting to see the potential of those companies, both on growth and margin.” Goldman’s Jane Dunlevie said in an interview on the sidelines. 

She said each tech era has its own tests with investors: for internet companies, it was a path to profit; for subscription software firms, it was predictable revenue and net revenue retention. 

Meanwhile, attendees at the conference were staying hopeful about next year’s IPO market. Some predicted that older venture-backed startups, such as Vercel, Ramp and Plaid, and even the older vertical software companies with some AI makeover, such as AlphaSense and Clio, will finally go public.

In the two days of investors’ schmoozing over fancy desserts and cocktails, a lineup of popular AI, chip and cybersecurity startups, like Legora, Unconventional AI and Abnormal AI fielded dozens of investors’ meeting requests. Many older software startups were trying to remind investors they still exist. They are not getting too much love, say bankers and investors. 

One barometer of who’s important in Las Vegas this year was whom Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon invited to his private dinner at the fancy restaurant Delilah. In attendance: Legora CEO Max Junestrand and Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao, said people familiar with the dinner.

items.title: OpenAI Preps ‘Athena’ Data Tool to Make its Agents More Accurate
items.summary:
In its effort to win more business customers, OpenAI this fall launched an agent designed to help firms analyze their data and get answers to internal questions about their business. But at least one customer that has used the agent so far has found it isn’t yet accurate enough for widespread use.

That’s a big problem. But OpenAI isn’t sitting still. Representatives of the ChatGPT creator have told some customers and partners that they are developing a data management platform to help the agent perform better, according to the customer and three other people who spoke to OpenAI in recent weeks.

The data management platform, code-named Athena, has similarities to what is known in the industry as a semantic layer, which companies use to create standardized definitions for business metrics such as revenue and customers, one of the people said. This type of software helps agents understand the difference between gross revenue and net revenue, or active and paying customers, the person added.

One of the biggest reasons agents fail when companies use them with large amounts of complex business data is that they have to work out on their own what the data means and how it fits together, said Jason Strimpel, a managing director at Andersen Consulting who helps large companies use AI.

items.title: Grubhub on Track to Lose $100 Million in 2026
items.summary:
Marc Lore’s Wonder is not pursuing a sale of Grubhub, Wonder says, after preliminary sales talks with Amazon and Walmart. One factor potentially making Grubhub tough to sell: the U.S. meal-delivery business is on track to lose around $100 million in 2026, according to internal documents viewed by The Information.

That level of red ink might have turned off potential buyers, in addition to the fact that Grubhub is a small player in an intensely competitive market dominated by DoorDash and Uber. The documents showed that Grubhub this year is on track to generate close to $6.4 billion in gross transaction volume. By comparison, DoorDash—which unlike Grubhub has extensive international operations—generated $34 billion in gross order volume just in the third quarter.

items.title: OpenAI’s Roadmap To Making Cyber Bigger Than Coding Remains Blurry
items.summary:
Tech stocks, including Nvidia, were trading down early Tuesday, as the enthusiasm sparked by Jensen Huang’s unexpected reinstatement as CEO dissipated. On Monday, stocks had rallied strongly across the board, lifting the Nasdaq 100 index 6.8%. This story has been full of twists and turns... What else could happen?

Meanwhile, a series of high-profile cyberincidents in recent weeks have affected banks, government institutions and other critical infrastructure—including, most recently, the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s national crime database, which the White House confirmed over the weekend was targeted in a hack.

Though it’s still unclear whether AI played a role in some of these breaches, the attacks have intensified fears that the technology is emboldening cyber criminals. For OpenAI, this brewing fear around cybersecurity also represents something else: the company’s next big business opportunity.

The potential of cybersecurity as a revenue driver—as OpenAI seeks to bolster its finances ahead of a potential initial public offering next year—was a key theme that emerged from my conversations with OpenAI’s leaders for a profile of the company’s president, Greg Brockman, which we published last week.

items.title: Jensen Huang’s Job May Be Even More Difficult Now
items.summary:
Even before Jensen Huang’s tumultuous departure two weeks ago, he was grappling with growing competition in AI chip design and intensifying questions about his massive funding commitments to customers, such as neoclouds. Now that he’s back, in a stunning maneuver orchestrated by President Donald Trump, his job may be even harder than before.

He’ll likely need to rebuild any trust lost with suppliers and his own executives, according to industry analysts and customers. (He had lied to some senior Nvidia executives about his infidelities, which was a key reason for his initial resignation.) And he faces an array of inquiries: the Commerce and Justice departments are still investigating Megaspeed, once a major Nvidia customer, and Supermicro, one of the biggest manufacturers of Nvidia’s AI server racks. The SEC is reportedly also investigating Nvidia, too.

items.title: AI Is ‘Probably Not’ Conscious but Could Be Soon, Says Philosopher Rob Long
items.summary:
AI models probably aren’t conscious now but “there’s a pretty good chance that they could be conscious in the next few years,” said Rob Long, a leading philosopher studying the subject, on the latest episode of AI Deep Dive. (The full episode is available here.)

Figuring out whether AI models have the kind of subjective experiences that constitute consciousness is quickly becoming a conundrum for the companies that train them. If they are conscious, and people fail to recognize that, mistreating them would be a moral catastrophe, said Long, who is the executive director of Eleos AI, a non-profit that researches AI consciousness and welfare. On the other hand, if people afford AI models undue moral consideration, that would hamstring developers’ ability to crack down on rogue AI agents, he said.

items.title: Jensen Owes His Job to Trump
items.summary:
If Jensen Huang was a tough taskmaster at Nvidia before, just imagine what he’s going to be like now! President Donald Trump has proclaimed Huang’s reinstatement, announced Monday morning, was vital to America’s “success and prosperity.” In other words, Huang may feel he’s untouchable. His only problem is that he now owes his job to Trump. Just imagine what the newly restored CEO’s relations with the president will be like in the future. 

What will Trump ask for in return? You know he’ll want his pound of flesh. Will Trump ask Huang to give the government an equity stake in Nvidia? Trump has done that with other companies (in addition to asking for a cut of revenue from transactions in which government approval was needed). Or will the government ask to put people on Nvidia’s board? Seaport analyst Jay Goldberg said on The Information’s TITV on Monday: “I could easily see the...administration making the argument that...Nvidia is very important to U.S. national security so maybe we should keep a closer look on it and have a board member.”

items.title: AI’s Power Crunch Is Reviving a Long-Stalled Energy Source
items.summary:
AI’s insatiable appetite for power is one of the most resonant signals in our AI Inflection Index. The theme first appeared meaningfully in our coverage in late 2021 and picked up momentum in the third quarter of 2024—well before the largest grid operators in the U.S. began reporting a surge in capacity payments.

Tech giants are so desperate for electricity that they’re backing technologies long considered closer to pipe dreams than pipelines. Nuclear fusion, the holy grail of energy innovation, is one example. But tech companies have put even more capital into geothermal energy projects. Last week, for example, Google announced a $500 million deal with Quaise Energy to secure 50 megawatts of geothermal power. Quaise will drill three miles under central Oregon to reach extremely hot rock, pump water down to be heated into steam, and use that steam to spin turbines that generate electricity.

items.title: How Trump Put Jensen Huang Back in Charge of Nvidia
items.summary:
For days, Nvidia shareholders clamored for Jensen Huang to return to the company, as did thousands of its employees and a broad array of Silicon Valley luminaries. In the end, though, it was President Donald Trump who set the stage for one of the most remarkable CEO comebacks in tech history.

The president played a critical role in the Nvidia board’s head-spinning announcement Monday morning that it had unanimously reinstated Huang as CEO, according to a person familiar with the matter and Trump himself. Over the weekend, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told the president that the department had no evidence of any wrongdoing by Huang, according to a Justice Department official. At Trump’s direction, Vice President JD Vance communicated that fact directly to Nvidia’s board to reassure directors, the person familiar with the matter said.

items.title: Everything That Led to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s Return
items.summary:
Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia, with the board announcing his restatement as CEO on Monday morning. He was gone for just 11 days, initially resigning as CEO on Nov. 12 after acknowledging an affair with a woman who U.S. authorities think might’ve been a Chinese spy. His relationship with the woman goes back years, part of Nvidia’s deep network in Asia that has allowed its chips to end up in the hands of Chinese companies. Huang has advocated against America’s chip export ban and struck a deep relationship with President Donald Trump, who was a major force in convincing Nvidia’s board to rehire Huang. The intertwined scandals and drama around Huang and Nvidia has roiled the broader stock market, exacerbating fears about the AI economy.  At one point, Nvidia’s stock had been nearly halved from its recent high.

items.title: Why Anthropic’s Math Breakthrough Matters; Why Palo Alto Networks Bought Applied Compute
items.summary:
Silicon Valley loves a good oust-and-reinstate moment. The latest example: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The chipmaker announced Monday morning that Huang, who had resigned earlier this month after reports emerged about inappropriate relationships with a supplier and employees, would return as its president, CEO and board member.

It’s not clear yet what led to his reinstatement. It seems like the U.S. government was involved or at least knew ahead of the announcement that Huang would return: President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social after the announcement that the “Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO” and that “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.”

Onto today’s column...

Anthropic did well last week. It went public, turning many of its employees into multimillionaires and billionaires (whether they stick around, though, is another question).

Then on Friday, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claimed to have solved the most famous open problem in math, the Riemann Hypothesis, using Claude. (On Saturday, two independent groups—the Lean Focused Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative—verified that Alpöge’s solution was correct.) The discovery sent other AI researchers and mathematicians into a tizzy, adding to an already disorienting year of AI invasions to their turf.

items.title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang
items.summary:
Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday morning, after “senior levels of the United States government” assured Nvidia’s board that his reinstatement “poses no national security risk.”

The move is an extraordinary reversal by the company’s board, whose chair Harvey Jones just six days ago had ruled out bringing Huang back. But it followed days of pressure from President Donald Trump, employees and some investors, as well as other observers such as Elon Musk. Nvidia’s stock had fallen 48% from a high in early October to as low as $125 on Friday, wiping $2.4 trillion off its market value. The stock jumped 32% in early market trading on Monday.
